2026-09-15.sessionName: Agents, context, MCP
Another one writes the code
2026-09-15.description: Generative AI can now write code across the data science lifecycle and produce plausible interpretations, challenging core assumptions about what beginners should learn and how they should be assessed. This talk examines the redesign of an introductory data science course at Duke University in response to these shifts. Some changes were made because of AI, including new in-class assessments; others were made thanks to AI, such as integrating just-in-time feedback in the IDE. I will discuss what changed, what failed, what improved, and how student feedback—ranging from enthusiasm to skepticism—is shaping an evolving approach to teaching data science in the age of generative AI.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Teaching at the frontier
What context do your AI agents actually need?
2026-09-15.description:
Context window! AGENTS.md! Custom instructions! Agent skills! Max tokens??

If you use AI agents in your data science work, you've probably heard tips about these things and already use some of them. But does it actually feel like your agents have the context they need about your data, packages, and analysis? Or do you find yourself re-explaining your data, spending more time editing agent output than doing the actual task, or using up tokens faster than you'd like?

Drawing on experience building Positron's agent features, this talk covers how to manage context: what kinds matter (from data to project structure), how to include them (files you write in advance vs. fetching info on the fly), and how to get results you don't have to rewrite.

2026-09-15.sessionName: AI Agents Deserve R
2026-09-15.description: R users have deep domain knowledge and finely-tuned workflows. You should not have to abandon them to use AI. The R ecosystem already has incredible building blocks: ellmer, shinychat, ragnar, and more. This talk will cover some new entrants that such as deputy, dsprrr, and shinymcp that grow the stack. Built on ellmer, deputy adds agentic workflows. This includes agents that plan, use tools, and solve multi-step tasks. dsprrr lets you program, not prompt, your LLM pipelines. Compose modules and let data-driven optimization tune for you. With coding agents making it easier than ever to port innovations across languages, R's AI story has never been stronger. Stay in an ecosystem you love and bring agents with you.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Public Policy in the Age of Demographic Uncertainty
2026-09-15.description:
This talk showcases a dashboard that creates demographic projections for regions across the United State of America to help drive impactful policies aimed at creating better human outcomes. The tool leverages the power of spatial statistics in R, Shiny, and the Apache Arrow ecosystem to efficiently provide regionally specific insights.

Forecasts and projections are always challenging, however federal policy uncertainty and an ongoing erosion to data quality are impeding our ability to plan for the future. This talk discusses the headwinds to demographic data creation and dissemination at the federal level and the implications this could have for local jurisdictions to provide key services to their communities.

2026-09-15.sessionName: MCP, or not MCP
2026-09-15.description: Model Context Protocol is a standard for defining tools that can be made available to LLMs and AI applications. There’s a lot of noise out there about what you should use to get the best results from AI, so in this talk, I will provide some guidance on when you should use MCP, and when you should reach for some other tool. I will describe cases where MCP is the right tool for the job, and when other things, like skills or other context files, are better. I will also devote attention to questions of security and authentication, which are important for MCP. Some critics of MCP have argued that they are risky, and I’ll discuss why. Then, I will show how you can use MCP in a way that actually improves your security and will delight IT admins.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Outgrowing Spreadsheets: Rebuilding Research Data Collection with Shiny and Posit Connect
2026-09-15.description: I’ll share how our nonprofit research team transformed a fragile, spreadsheet-based data collection process into a sustainable system using Shiny and Posit Connect. We publish a data set on 2,500 hospital financial assistance programs and how they collect medical debt from patients. Our team collected this data using Google Forms and sheets. It technically worked, but it was fragile, slow, and completely dependent on one person (me). When we finally got Posit Connect, we rebuilt the system based on three principles: structured data entry, automated validation, and recorded updates. This talk shares the before-and-after architecture and practical lessons for teams ready to outgrow spreadsheets and design sustainable workflows.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Dashboards
Organization-wide goodies
The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Quarto
2026-09-15.description: Quarto markets itself as a publishing framework. But at its core, Quarto is an abstraction layer separating *content* from *format* — a distinction that turns out to be remarkably powerful in the era of AI agents. When an LLM generates a document, content and structure emerge together in a single probabilistic pass, but nothing in that output is guaranteed. Quarto's code-at-render-time model solves this by letting the LLM build the structure while allowing the content that must be exact to be rendered deterministically from data files. The result is reproducible and auditable output that stays correct as your content changes, without needing to re-prompt models. This talk brings the agent + Quarto workflow to life with concrete examples, from a simple one-page PDF to a fully interactive multi-page dashboard integrating JavaScript libraries, Shinylive, and React, showing how asking an LLM for a qmd file instead of a finished document dramatically reduces token overhead while producing more dynamic, trustworthy, and maintainable output.

speakers.title: Associate Professor, The George Washington University
speakers.description: John Paul (JP) is an Associate Professor at George Washington University in the Department of Engineering Management and Systems Engineering. His research focuses on understanding how consumer preferences, market dynamics, and policy affect the emergence and adoption of low-carbon technologies, such as electric vehicles and renewable energy technologies. He also studies the critical relationship between the US and China in developing and mass producing these technologies. He has expertise in exploratory data analysis, data visualization, reproducible workflows, choice modeling, conjoint analysis, survey design, interview-based research methods, the R programming language, China, and the global electric vehicle industry. He speaks fluent Mandarin Chinese and has conducted extensive fieldwork in China. John holds a Ph.D. and M.S. in Engineering and Public Policy from Carnegie Mellon University and a B.S. in Engineering Science and Mechanics (ESM) from Virginia Tech.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Say Yes to the Request - From Helping One to Empowering Many
2026-09-15.description: R adoption surged when we embraced one rule: say yes to every question and turn each insight into something that lasts. To hit GSK’s 50% R-by-2026 goal, STARburst—a small team of R experts—opened a helpdesk focused on high-touch support. Each interaction followed a deliberate user journey: we met people where they were, unblocked the immediate task, then used that same moment to teach reusable habits for open-source ways of working. In parallel, we logged every learning and gap, turning recurring issues into R and Quarto assets: daily blogs and FAQs first, then example libraries, hardened guidance, and improved R packages. Attendees will see how bite-sized, one-to-one help compounds into organization-wide R capability for the long haul.

speakers.title: Data Scientist, GSK
speakers.description: Becca Krouse is a data scientist in GSK’s Statistics and Data Science Innovation Hub where she focuses on enabling users across R&D. A biostatistician by training, she has experience spanning over 15 years in the field of clinical research and specializes in developing R-based tools.

2026-09-15.sessionName: SQL as a first-class language in your data science IDE
2026-09-15.description: Data scientists spend a lot of time and effort writing SQL, yet most data science environments treat it as an afterthought or a separate workflow, forcing you to switch tools, copy results between windows, and lose context along the way. In this talk, learn how Positron brings SQL into the same environment where you write Python and R code. We’ll walk through connecting to databases, writing queries with intelligent code completion, executing SQL in a dedicated console, and exploring results in the Data Explorer. You’ll see how keeping SQL alongside your other data science work reduces friction and errors. This talk is for data scientists and analysts who regularly query databases and want to stop context-switching between tools.

2026-09-15.sessionName: A Grammar of Graphics for SQL
2026-09-15.description: SQL has been with us for many years, but despite its age it is still a cornerstone of data-analysis everywhere. The quick success of DuckDB shows this more than ever. However,  SQL is often used as the first step to extract data, delegating any search for insight to a different programming language or environment. I would like to present ggsql, an extension of SQL that provides a grammar of graphics on top of SQL and allows you to create visualisations directly within your query. ggsql is a modular tool, build to interface directly with your data source and optimised for use by an LLM based data analysis workflow due to its lack of runtime.

2026-09-15.sessionName: One Report, Many Audiences: Role‑Based Views in Posit Connect
2026-09-15.description: Harvard University’s decentralized structure creates diverse data needs across its many schools. Our central institutional research office uses Posit Connect to share data and reports, but not every person should see the same content. To address this, we published a Shiny app on Posit Connect that detects the logged‑in user and dynamically tailors what they see. This means that a single report can securely serve many audiences. This talk will walk through how the pieces fit together and offer a model for organizations seeking scalable, user‑aware reporting.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Quarto Wiki Chatbot
2026-09-15.description: After a year of compiling onboarding, technical, and other documentation into a centralized Quarto Wiki, NASA’s People Analytics team still struggled to quickly search for needed information. We developed an integrated chatbot, which surfaces and cites relevant content to answer user questions - processing QMD files into a vector database, developing a Python RAG pipeline, and embedding an R Shiny chat window into the Quarto site’s interface. To reduce latency and long-term LLM costs, DuckDB caches and scores prior query-response pairs for selective reuse. The system can be deployed on Posit Connect or run locally, illustrating a reproducible workflow for interactive, AI-assisted documentation. Presented by: Aliza Samad and Sofia Lendahl.

speakers.title: AI/ML Research Associate, NASA
speakers.description:
Hi! I recently graduated from the University of California, Santa Barbara with a B.S. in Statistics and Data Science. I've been working on AI applications and tools with NASA for the past 1.5 years. I love learning about machine learning techniques and the latest in AI innovation. My other interests include hiking, reading, and music!

Feel free to connect with me!

2026-09-15.sessionName: Template → Package → App: Meeting Users Where They're At
2026-09-15.description: We built a reporting workflow to help farmers turn complex soil health data into useful management decisions. What started as a Quarto template for one specific project became the {soils} R package for other coders, and eventually Dirt Data Reports, a Shiny app for people who don't code. This talk is about what we learned while lowering barriers at each step. Building for the user means choosing the right level of flexibility, abstraction, and complexity for the people you're trying to reach. The goal isn't to create one perfect tool; it's to meet users where they're at.

speakers.title: Data Scientist, Washington State Department of Agriculture
speakers.description: Jadey Ryan is a Data Scientist at the Washington State Department of Agriculture, where she manages data, builds automated reporting workflows, and develops decision support tools using R, Quarto, and Shiny. Her work supports the Washington Soil Health Initiative and focuses on making complex data more accessible and actionable for agricultural and environmental applications.

2026-09-15.sessionName: SQL Without Writing SQL: dbplyr for Serious Shiny Apps
2026-09-15.description: You don't need to be an SQL expert or a DBA to build high-performance Shiny apps on large datasets. With dbplyr, you can write familiar dplyr code while it translates your pipelines into optimized SQL behind the scenes. In this talk we will explore how integrating Shiny with Postgres SQL and how the dplyr you write today can translate to better performing applications. We will cover practical patterns to keep computation in the database to create production-ready apps without leaving R.

speakers.title: Principal Data Science Analyst, Mayo Clinic

2026-09-15.sessionName: Keynote Session: How to Be Clear When You Can’t Be Certain
2026-09-15.description: Sometimes, data visualization is about using charts to illustrate a key point or conclusion gleaned from analyzing the data. But what if you’re not sure what the conclusion is? Presenting examples from news reporting on the topics of elections, polling and economics, I will talk about how I have grappled with uncertainty and how to communicate it to the public.

speakers.title: Graphics Editor, New York Times
speakers.description: Christine Zhang is a New York Times reporter specializing in graphics and data journalism. Her work has informed many of The Times’s election-related projects, including the election night Needle, the graphics accompanying the release of every New York Times Times/Siena College poll, and the map showing the most detailed results of the 2024 presidential election. Before working in news, she was a research analyst at The Brookings Institution, where she made her first real foray into R, and she also spent a few years in finance. She contributes periodically to The Times’s Business section, most recently in her coverage of the Federal Reserve. Between elections and the economy, she has no shortage of ideas to consider when trying to bring clarity to complex (and occasionally esoteric) topics.

2026-09-15.sessionName: For the community, by the community: The 10-year journey of R Weekly powered by open-source
2026-09-15.description: For a decade, R Weekly has highlighted the innovations, creativity, and novel resources tailored to the R language across data science. Built and sustained by a small, volunteer curator team, the project demonstrates how open-source values—transparency, collaboration, and shared ownership—can power a lasting community initiative. This talk explores how R Weekly evolved, the workflows and infrastructure that keep it running, and the lessons learned from ten years of amplifying innovation. This talk will demonstrate how community-driven curation can strengthen ecosystems and inspire sustainable open-source contributions.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Interdependent Filters in Shiny Made Simple
2026-09-15.description:
Developing interdependent filters in Shiny has always been tedious, requiring 
developers to rewrite custom ui and server logic for each new app. The new R 
package shinyfilters exists to eliminate this boilerplate. shinyfilters lets 
anyone create interdependent filters directly from data.frames. I am excited to 
show attendees how shinyfilters uses S7 to simplify interdependent filter logic, 
how to replace repetitive ui and server code with simple function calls, and 
how to extend shinyfilters for their own use cases.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Beyond Bootstrap: Building Custom Shiny UI Packages with AI
2026-09-15.description:
Shiny developers have long been limited to Bootstrap and a handful of pre-built UI frameworks. But what if you could use Material UI, Ant Design, or any modern react.js web framework you love?

This talk demonstrates how AI can generate production-ready R packages that wrap your favorite UI frameworks for Shiny. We'll walk through using AI to translate JavaScript components into R bindings, handle dependencies, and create idiomatic interfaces—no JavaScript expertise required.

You'll see live examples, learn effective prompting patterns, and discover how to maintain AI-generated packages. Whether you want Material Design or Web Components, AI makes it possible to bring any UI framework into your Shiny apps.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Quarto Notebooks and Literate Programming in Positron
2026-09-15.description: Quarto Notebooks, a new Positron feature, give you access to Jupyter's literate programming features without losing any of the benefits of working with plain text for editing, versioning, and collaborating. They are a natural evolution of the R Markdown Notebooks feature in RStudio into the modern, multi-lingual environment of Quarto and Positron. In this talk, I'll introduce this new way of working, and describe both its similarities and differences to its predecessor in RStudio. Finally, we'll spend some time comparing the different tools for literate programming in Positron, their tradeoffs, and how to choose the right one.

2026-09-15.sessionName: ADBC: A Faster Foundation for Database Connectivity in R, Python, and Beyond
2026-09-15.description: dplyr was a revolution for R, and dbplyr was a smaller but important revolution for those of us who wanted to use databases without leaving behind the powerful and familiar syntax of dplyr. The arrow R package was another revolution of its own, letting us work with larger-than-memory data while still using dplyr syntax. Apache Arrow, the larger project of which the arrow R package is a part, also has a standard for database access: ADBC. In this talk, I’ll introduce ADBC, which works with R, Python, and other languages and is coming to dbplyr. I’ll give an intro to Arrow and ADBC, and show how to use a new command line tool, dbc, along with dbplyr, for fast, larger-than-memory database access that works seamlessly across R and Python.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Shiny in Pieces
The Notebook
Yes And...AI in Your IDE
2026-09-15.description: Large language models are now embedded in our IDEs, shaping how we code. Research suggests assistants don’t respond “neutrally”: how you ask and even cues about who is asking can shift what the model says. In this session, we’ll explore what that looks like with Posit’s AI tools that draw on IDE context. We’ll run simple “paired prompts”: same problem, different asker then compare their agreement, and whether the assistant challenges assumptions or amplifies them. This talk is about using LLMs while involving the user, and bringing in the decision-making before the result. Bring curiosity, your critical thinking, and a healthy suspicion of anything that agrees with you a little too easily.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Shiny design: Where humans and AI disagree
2026-09-15.description: AI can generate Shiny dashboards, grade visual quality from screenshots, and tweak their own code. But do they actually like the same designs people do? We pitted automated visual scores against blind human rankings across dashboards built by different models, frameworks, and prompts. I'll share where machine taste matches human judgment, where it completely falls off, and what these gaps tell us about visual design. Finally, we'll look at how human input can spot the flaws in automated scoring so we can build far better AI evaluators.

speakers.title: QA Engineer, Posit PBC
speakers.description: Karan is a Senior Quality Assurance Engineer at Posit, where he works on Shiny. He has worked with tech startups across the San Francisco Bay Area, helping them ship products efficiently without compromising on quality. In his spare time, he takes part in BioBlitzes around the Bay Area and contributes to this natural history blog.

2026-09-15.sessionName: From Tribal Knowledge to Trusted AI in Pharma
2026-09-15.description:
Everyone wants to know how to build useful AI. We learned that the hardest part wasn’t the technical implementation at all.

We expected embeddings, entity extraction, retrieval pipelines, and plenty of AI plumbing. Instead, the work that mattered most was sitting with pharmaceutical sales reps, uncovering tribal knowledge, resolving conflicting definitions, and turning years of business logic from Shiny apps on Posit Connect into governed logic in Snowflake.

This talk shows what changed once we built around how people actually work. We’ll share how user feedback shaped the language, rules, UX, and priorities of the system, and how that human context made the AI more trustworthy, explainable, and useful in the field.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Influence with Quarto: Designing Reports That Drive Decisions
2026-09-15.description: Most people using Quarto already know how to render documents. This talk focuses on what comes next: elevating Quarto reports through design, layout, and narrative. Using a realistic example report, I’ll show how styling, visual hierarchy, and thoughtful structure can transform a technically correct analysis into a compelling story for decision-makers. The goal isn’t more code, but better communication: using the right data storytelling, CSS, and ggplot to create reports that feel intentional, polished, and impactful. Attendees will leave with concrete ideas to push their own Quarto reports beyond defaults.

speakers.title: Lead Data Scientist, Cleo
speakers.description:
Lead Data Scientist specializing in product analytics, experimentation and AI-driven decision making. Throughout her career at Apple, and now Cleo, she has helped product teams transform complex data into actionable business decisions.

Beyond her day-to-day work, Paula is passionate about data communication. She writes the blog *El Arte del Dato Bien Contado*, where she explores practical techniques for designing visualizations that help stakeholders understand evidence and make confident decisions.

At posit::conf 2026, she shares lessons learned from years of building analytical products for global technology companies, showing how Quarto can be used not only to create beautiful reports, but to influence decisions.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Repotting and propagating my Shiny houseplant
2026-09-15.description: My Shiny app started out as a single seed: one app.R. Its quick growth became restricted by its tiny pot as features tangled together. So, I repotted my app.R file into 11 modules to organize my UI and server logic. My Shiny plant kept growing, but with better structure. To share my thriving plant with friends and clients, I learned how to propagate cuttings to create new, similar apps by turning it into a package. This let me reuse the core code across apps, while making pieces customizable. To update calculations or aesthetics, I now update the package code once, rather than editing 10 different apps. This talk will walk through the app growth cycle, what triggers each step, and how to repot and propagate without killing your Shiny plant.

speakers.title: Drinking Water Engineer, Brown and Caldwell

2026-09-15.sessionName: Hello, robot: Introducing humans to LLM’s
2026-09-15.description: You know that AI can be transformative when used correctly, but how do you train your team – or organization – to be effective AI users? Last year we tackled this problem through a course that built foundational LLM skills for staff at Posit. By focusing on learner curiosity, personal experience and experimentation, we helped teams across the organization develop relevant skills with AI tools. In this talk, I'll share some details of our approach, lessons we learned, and ideas on how to scale this type of learning within an organization; I will also debut a publicly-accessible version of the course.

speakers.title: Manager, Academy Apprenticeships, Posit, PBC
speakers.description: Kristin Bott manages the Posit Academy Apprenticeship program, which is focused on building both coding and collaboration skills in working professionals. Kristin brings a background in natural science, organizing, teaching, and research, and spent 10 years in higher ed before joining Posit in 2021. She is passionate about making technical topics accessible through the power of learning communities, with the goal of empowering individuals to do great work.

2026-09-15.sessionName: High Quality R/Shiny Apps at Scale: Lessons from DaVinci’s Modular Framework
2026-09-15.description: Scaling R/Shiny apps is hard: code gets duplicated, UX becomes inconsistent, and validation is expensive. With DaVinci, a Shiny framework for exploring clinical trial data, we address these issues through a modular approach. DaVinci provides reusable, qualified modules that follow shared standards for structure, interfaces, testing, and performance. This talk shows why modularity works at scale, how it speeds up delivery and improves quality, and how module developers, app creators, and app users work together to build robust apps. Attendees will learn practical patterns to improve consistency, maintainability, and validation effort – applicable to any team building many Shiny apps, not only in pharma.

speakers.title: Senior Clinical Data Engineer, Boehringer Ingelheim

2026-09-15.sessionName: From chats to workflows to “agents”: Demystifying LLM jargon by example
2026-09-15.description:
If the phrase "agentic AI" has ever made you scratch your head (or roll your eyes), this talk is for you. The AI field is awash in jargon that sounds precise but isn't—and when every technology is branded as an "agent" or "agentic," it’s pretty hard to know what anyone is talking about. So, let's fix that. 

In this gentle, no-experience-required introduction to LLM systems, I'll demystify the jargon by building up from first principles. Using a single running example—turning messy clinical notes into a structured summary—we'll walk through four levels of LLM system design: chats, workflows, agents, and multi-agent systems. You'll leave with a better understanding of agentic design patterns and how to try them out for yourself.

speakers.title: Senior Data Scientist, Stanford Health Care

2026-09-15.sessionName: Lightning Talks
Better Notebooks with Marimo: Reproducible Data Science Workflows
2026-09-15.description:
Interactive notebooks are foundational in applied data science, but they introduce their own problems: out-of-order execution, difficult storage formats, and input-output mixing. Marimo is a modern Python notebook system that tackles these problems head-on. Reactive execution ensures reproducibility, its script-based format works well with version control and a broader Python codebase, and its outputs stay separate from inputs.

But Marimo offers even more. This talk will show how Marimo notebooks fit naturally into analytics projects, focusing both on code features—pytest compatibility and its Python script format—and editor features, including a VS Code extension, LLM support, and Quarto integration.

2026-09-15.sessionName: The modern tool builder: CLIs, agents, and PEP 723
2026-09-15.description:
Being able to write R or Python scripts is an incredibly useful skill, allowing you to automate nearly any task imaginable. However, with a bit of extra effort, those brittle scripts can be transformed into robust, reusable tools. In particular, tools that you can run from the command line or that can be run by coding agents. Future-you will thank you for making the extra effort.

In this talk, we will explore why you should graduate from writing scripts to building tools, particularly command-line interfaces (CLIs).

CLIs have been around for over 50 years. Thanks to the rise of coding agents, being able to understand and use the command line is now more important than ever. I'd say there are three reasons for this. First, coding agents rely on CLI tools such as find, grep, and git (and maybe yours!). Second, some coding agents, such as Claude Code, are themselves CLI tools that you can incorporate into your scripts. Third, agents are actually really good at helping you to build your own tools, so if you use them there's really no excuse anymore.

speakers.title: Head of Developer Relations, Posit
speakers.description: Jeroen Janssens, PhD, is Head of Developer Relations at Posit, PBC. His expertise lies in visualizing data, implementing machine learning models, and building solutions using Python, R, JavaScript, and Bash. He’s passionate about open source and sharing knowledge. He’s the author of Python Polars: The Definitive Guide (O’Reilly, 2025) and Data Science at the Command Line (O’Reilly, 2021). Jeroen holds a PhD in machine learning from Tilburg University and an MSc in artificial intelligence from Maastricht University. He lives with his wife and two kids in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Positron and the Three Bears: Teaching Python with Positron
2026-09-15.description:
For polyglot data science, RStudio is too specific, VS Code is too general, but Positron is just right. However, it’s not without friction. With two years of experience teaching Python with Positron, I’ll discuss how Positron fits in the data stack and how it helps address the “three bears” of teaching Python:

1. Installing Python and managing virtual environments
2. Creating GitHub-friendly notebook workflows
3. Accessing scalable compute resources

I hope my experience with Positron can help other attendees in their professional and personal efforts as instructors and mentors.

2026-09-15.sessionName: The Modern Data Science Stack... still SQL
Delivering Automations at Scale: {rtemplate} for High‑Throughput Biomarker Analytics
2026-09-15.description: Supporting hundreds of biomarker focused clinical and exploratory studies requires fast, standardized, and reproducible early stage analyses in the biopharma industry. After exploring approaches and needs of analysts and scientists, our team converged on {rtemplate} - an R based automation framework that easily delivers structured data via {arrow}, an orchestrated analysis pipeline via {targets}, consistent figure standards via {ggplot2}, and Quarto powered {shiny} viewers. With by AI assisted feature development, {rtemplate} enables teams to meet tight timelines while shifting analyst time toward the deep, high impact scientific work that matches the reality of clinical and exploratory biomarker workloads. Developed in collaboration with Peter Ehmann, previously with Regeneron, now with Merck & Co., Inc.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Making the Impossible Possible: A Software-First Stack for Resource-Constrained Research
2026-09-15.description: At Drexel's Urban Health Collaborative, we study how climate change affects health across US and Latin American cities — complex work run by a small team with no enterprise budget. I'll share how Posit's code-first products took us from ad hoc data management to a software-first organization. Starting from RStudio, Quarto turned pipelines into reproducible notebooks and Positron opened the door to Python tools like dbt-DuckDB. That let us adopt analytics engineering, GitHub-driven development, and Notion for non-technical collaboration — shipping model-ready data fast. This code-first stack is ready for what's next: agentic AI. Attendees leave with a playbook for a lightweight data stack resource-constrained teams can adopt incrementally.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Small Team Doing Big Things
From Programming Alone to Programming and Prompting: Teaching Bilingual AI-Enabled Data Science with Positron and Quarto
2026-09-15.description: Most courses teach R or Python. I teach both—in the same Quarto documents, using Positron. Students start with parallel tracks (bag-of-words, NLP in both languages), then shift mid-semester to integrated workflows: R for preprocessing, Python for transformers. But I've moved beyond programming alone. Prompt engineering starts week two. GitHub Copilot and Positron Assistant are available from day one, with prompting exercises in every lab. These bilingual, AI-augmented skills are essential. One surprise: students with no prior programming experience end up more bilingual than those who arrive knowing one language. No home base to retreat to. I'll share what's working, what's not, and how Positron and Quarto make this practical.

speakers.title: Professor and Executive Director, American University
speakers.description:
Derrick L. Cogburn is a Full Professor at American University's School of International Service (SIS), where he is housed in the Department of Environment, Development & Health. Dr. Cogburn holds a joint appointment in the Kogod School of Business in the Department of Information Technology & Analytics. He holds a UNESCO Associate Chair on Transnational Challenges and Governance and directs both the Institute on Disability and Public Policy (IDPP) and the Internet Governance Lab (IGL). He also co-chairs the Global Academic Network for the Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP).

Dr. Cogburn's research applies computational methods—including text mining, machine learning, social network analysis, and retrieval-augmented generation—to international human rights and disability policy. His current work focuses on UN human rights monitoring mechanisms, particularly the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) treaty body processes. His applied work includes the CRPD Data Dashboard, a policy analytics platform developed with IDPP and Praxis Analytics AI, funded by the National Science Foundation through American University's Translating Research into Action Center (TRAC). He recently presented the dashboard at CRPD COSP-19 at the United Nations in New York, where his side event connected broader human rights accountability mechanisms to the CRPD treaty framework.

At American University, Dr. Cogburn teaches graduate courses in text analytics and AI policy, including ITEC/SIS 724: Large-Scale Text Analysis. In this course, he trains students to become bilingual R and Python programmers using Positron as their IDE and Quarto documents as their primary deliverable format. His pedagogical approach integrates prompt engineering from week two—not as an afterthought—with GitHub Copilot and Positron Assistant available from day one. He has found that students without prior programming experience often achieve stronger bilingual fluency than those who arrive with a single-language background, a counterintuitive finding that shapes his teaching philosophy. He has developed a new course for fall 2026 SIS 750 Applied AI for Global Challenges. 

Dr. Cogburn is currently developing a new graduate certificate at SIS titled "Global Challenges and Applied AI," anchored by his existing cross-listed courses and connected to IDPP, IGL, the UNESCO Chair, and CAIDP. He also runs Praxis Analytics AI, a consulting practice focused on applied computational social science and AI development for policy research, small businesses, and non-profit organizations.

Prior to joining American University, Dr. Cogburn held faculty positions in the Schools of Information at Syracuse University and the University of Michigan. He is a graduate of Howard University and the University of Oklahoma.

His professional identity is captured in three words: Scholar. Teacher. Sailor.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Designing Reproducible Learning Ecosystems with R and Quarto
2026-09-15.description: Reproducibility in data science is often taught as a final requirement rather than as a workflow that evolves over time. This talk presents a reproducible learning ecosystem built with R and Quarto that moves learners from one-off assignments to durable, public work—and ultimately into contributors. Learners iteratively refactor their analyses into portfolio books, contribute to a shared research volume built on real civic data, and engage with open tooling that lowers barriers to authentic analysis. The session focuses on design decisions, lessons learned, and practical patterns for teaching reproducibility through iteration, ownership, and real-world data.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Bridging the Gap: Custom Catalogs to Connect End Users with Data Products
2026-09-15.description: For data scientists today, creating stellar apps and reports is not enough without proper dissemination to the end users. Our team has created dozens of Shiny apps and Quarto reports which can be useful to the wider organization. Now, to bridge the gap between our users and data products, we have developed an interactive catalog with Quarto Dashboard, the connectapi R package, and a content tags hierarchy on Connect. We aim to help end-users explore our offerings and quickly find the tools they can most benefit from. My talk will demonstrate how any data analytics team can easily build their own custom catalog to better communicate with their end users.

2026-09-15.sessionName: The Tableau Plateau: From Dashboards to AI-Ready Data Products
2026-09-15.description: At Suffolk, we hit a “Tableau plateau.” Our team had split into two tribes: point-and-click dashboard builders and code-first data scientists. BI tools felt faster - but capped our technical ceiling. By standardizing on Shiny, using Git-backed deployment for Posit Connect, and leveraging AI coding agents like Positron Assistant, we flipped the equation. With Shiny modules and brand.yml providing guardrails for developers and agents, we standardized structure, styling, and patterns. Code not only surpassed point-and-click tools in speed - it produced extensible products built for ML and AI integration. This shift unified our team and transformed dashboards from reporting artifacts into AI-ready data products.

speakers.title: Sr Director, Data Product, Suffolk Construction

2026-09-15.sessionName: Posit Pro Product Updates
2026-09-15.description:
Join this special session to hear the latest product updates from Posit, including Posit Workbench, Connect, Package Manager, the Posit Team Native App for Snowflake, Connect Cloud, and Posit AI. This session will have 5 talks!

  • Trust in the Cloud: Secure Deployments and Effortless AI Access | Alex Chisholm | Posit
    Data science professionals and their teams face growing governance questions. What's been deployed, where the data lives, and which models have seen it. At the same time, they - and the system admins watching over it all - want the ease and speed that cloud deployments promise. Too often, speed and governance get treated as opposing goals, but they don't have to be.
    In this talk, we'll show how Connect Cloud and a Posit AI subscription are built to deliver both. Connect Cloud, now through its first SOC 2 Type 1 audit, lets you publish from RStudio, Positron, GitHub, or the command line, with scheduling and custom domains that empower everyone without the infrastructure overhead. A Posit AI subscription powers Posit Assistant and Next Edit Suggestions with a curated set of validated models, plus Zero Data Retention coverage and full control over your data so that speed and trust don't have to be a tradeoff.
    Not every organization can operate entirely in the cloud for every use case. But for the teams who can, we want to offer the easiest, safest choice possible.
  • Enterprise Data Science, Minus the Overhead: Posit Team Native App on Snowflake | Chetan Thapar | Posit
    If you're a data scientist at an enterprise running Posit's pro products, the odds are you aren't on a recent version. The products keep improving; the environment you actually work in updates once a year, if that. If you're the platform admin, you know why. Every upgrade is a project: infrastructure, coordination, downtime, security review. And standing the platform up in the first place was a bigger project still - infra, software, role provisioning - before a single data scientist ran their first analysis. The Posit Team Native App runs Workbench, Connect, and Package Manager natively inside your own Snowflake account. Access is instant: install from the Marketplace, start a self-service trial, and be working in minutes. Ops headaches go away: it's a fully managed service, upgrades arrive automatically and typically monthly, roles are inherited from Snowflake rather than provisioned twice, and your data never leaves your perimeter. And productivity compounds: your data scientists get the latest releases without the platform overhead; all three are wired to work together out of the box; and Posit Assistant runs on Cortex-hosted LLMs with semantic model awareness, no configuration required. Instant access, no ops headache, accelerated productivity. This session is what we've delivered against each of these recently, where we still have work to do, and what's coming next, including an early look at R MLOps on Snowflake.
  • Beyond Packages: Governing the AI Toolchain with Posit Package Manager | Joe Roberts | Posit
    Posit Package Manager started as a way to govern R and Python packages — mirroring, curating, and controlling what makes it into your environments. That job hasn't gone away, but it's no longer the whole story.
    As AI agents become part of everyday data science work, teams need the same governance discipline applied to a new set of artifacts: VS Code extensions, AI plugins, and the growing ecosystem of tools that agents use to get work done. In this talk, we'll look at how Package Manager is expanding to meet that need.
    We'll start with a practical overview of AI plugins — what they are, what capabilities they expose, and why curating them matters as much as curating packages. From there, we'll show how PPM acts as a private marketplace for these plugins, and how Posit Assistant and other AI agents can connect to that marketplace directly. Finally, we'll get hands-on with PPM's MCP server, showing how it makes agent-to-PPM integration straightforward, and how AI plugins themselves can define MCP servers hosted on Posit Connect and elsewhere — turning your governed package repository into a governed tool repository.
    You'll leave with a clear picture of where package management is headed as AI agents join the data science workflow, and concrete ideas for how to keep that expansion safe, curated, and useful.
  • Building Posit Connect for Two Very Different AI Organizations | Kelly O’Briant & Matt Leary | Posit
    As product managers of Posit Connect, we get to talk to a lot of different kinds of organizations about how they’re using AI. 
    Some have AI everywhere. Every department has its own assistants. There are dozens of chat applications, hundreds of prototypes, and new tools appearing faster than anyone can keep track of. Success has created a lot of questions: Who owns these applications? Which models are they using? What data can they access? Who is monitoring them?
    Others are still struggling to get started. People want to build AI-powered tools, but security, IT, and legal can't agree on how to move forward. The most ambitious employees find consumer AI tools on their own, while the most cautious wait for solutions or decisions that may never arrive. 
    These organizations look completely different. What they need, however, is remarkably similar.
    In this talk, I'll show how we're building Posit Connect to support both of these organizations. The details differ, but the destination is the same: a platform where anyone can publish useful AI-powered work, regardless of language or framework, while giving administrators the visibility and control they need to make AI sustainable across the organization.
  • AI Governance: Bringing Posit Assistant to the enterprise | Thomas Mock | Posit
    As data science teams rapidly integrate AI, the challenge lies not merely in achieving correct analysis, but in demonstrating that results are trustworthy and compliant. While tools like Posit Assistant bring powerful, code-first, and session-aware data science assistance to RStudio and Positron, many organizations struggle with implementation by retrofitting governance as a separate, friction-heavy layer.
    This presentation explores a shift toward architectural governance, integrating oversight directly into the infrastructure rather than applying it as an external control. We will demonstrate a model built on four core pillars: code-first design, human-in-the-loop workflows, session-aware data privacy, and governed environments. By leveraging unified infrastructure, we can align the needs of data scientists with the requirements of IT, compliance, and security teams. Attendees will learn how to move governance from an administrative burden to a seamless, inherent feature of the data science lifecycle.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Everything you wanted to know about agents* (*but were afraid to ask)
2026-09-15.description:
Agents, agents, agents. The practice of software development has been transformed by AI coding agents like Claude Code. The practice data science is also being changed by AI coding agents, but not quite in the same way. Data science uses many of the same tools and techniques as pure software development, but at its heart there is a fundamental difference: with software development, the goal is to build something, but with data analysis, the goal is to learn something.

With that in mind, I’ll talk about:
- What is an agent?
- How do they work?
- What are they good at, and what are they bad at?
- How is software development different from data science?
- How can you maximize your trust in agent’s work?

2026-09-15.sessionName: Being an informed and savvy AI user
Great Docs: Beautiful Documentation Sites for Python Packages
2026-09-15.description:
Documentation is one of the most impactful things you can do for your Python package (and one of the most tedious to set up). Between manually cataloging your API, wrestling with configuration, and keeping everything in sync as your code evolves, many projects ship with incomplete docs (or none).

Great Docs eliminates this friction. A single command auto-discovers your package's public API and generates a complete, professionally styled documentation site. It also auto-generates llms.txt files, creates license and citation pages, and gives you a polished landing page, organized API reference, and User Guide section.

In this talk, I'll introduce Great Docs, walk through its workflow, and demo sites I've built for several Python projects.

speakers.title: Software Engineer, Posit, PBC
speakers.description: Richard Iannone is a software engineer at Posit, PBC. He focuses on building open-source tools that help people work more effectively with data. In R, he works on several packages including gt, pointblank, and blastula. In Python, his focus is on Great Tables (a port of gt) and Great Docs (documentation-site generator for Python libraries).

2026-09-15.sessionName: Less to decide, more to reuse: the block in blockr
2026-09-15.description: We present blockr, a framework for interactively building data workflows, developed in collaboration with Bristol-Myers Squibb. Implemented as a modular set of R packages, blockr suits applications from interactive dashboards to static reports. The break-down into well-defined steps, along with AI assistance, provides a natural, no-code interface to complex problems. A block is a deliberately restricted unit of computation, and this is what lets the same blocks be reused across very different applications. We show what it takes to write a block. We then look at a production app built almost entirely from general-purpose blocks, with domain-specific ones only where the problem demands them, and an AI assistant to assemble them.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Debugging Is a Nightmare: Meaningful Metaphors for Data Science Education
2026-09-15.description: Metaphor and analogy are often treated as rhetorical flourishes, but they play a real role in how we learn technical concepts. In data science education, metaphors help make invisible processes visible and support transfer from familiar experience into abstract reasoning. This talk treats “debugging is a nightmare” as more than a phrase, using it to guide concrete practices like “dream journaling” (minimal reproducible examples), “lucid dreaming” (stepping through code), and “magic apples” (capturing state). It then steps back to reflect on how such frames shape learners’ reasoning, where they help, where they break down, and what educators should be deliberate about in choosing appropriate metaphors.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Finding Common Language between Data Scientists and Non Data Scientists
2026-09-15.description: Data scientists need to communicate effectively with stakeholders who do not have a programming background but do have detailed technical knowledge in an area where the data scientist is not an expert. Finding the right shared language helps minimize wasted work, especially early in a project. For example: cooking recipes can serve as an analogous data set understood by synthesis chemists and data scientists working on chemical reaction data. Use of a common language reduces the amount of brainpower spent interpreting terminology and allows everyone to focus on design goals – data visualizations, search interfaces, data sources, etc. This talk will provide advice for finding a shared language topic and examples of how they can be used.

speakers.title: Dow
speakers.description: Michael is a scientist in Research and Development at Dow where he works to ensure other researchers have ready access to data about products they wish to improve and potential ingredients to use in a formulation. He also enjoys helping researchers speed up their data analysis, often via creation of Shiny apps that turn structured-but-non-tidy analytical instrument outputs into graphs and tidy tables. Outside of work he spends much of his time bicycling and playing Ultimate in the summer and curling in the winter.

2026-09-15.sessionName: SELECT instance FROM cloud WHERE workload = ? ORDER BY cost_efficiency
2026-09-15.description:
Selecting the right cloud instance for DS/ML/AI workloads is still mostly guesswork. Pricing and hardware specs exist, but fragmented across providers and hard to compare, especially when real workload performance matters.

We introduce Spare Cores Navigator, an open dataset covering thousands of cloud instance types across vendors with standardized performance and cost-efficiency metrics. We show how instance choice becomes a simple data task in R or Python: filter by workload, hardware, compliance, or budget, then rank candidates by price-performance to identify the most efficient option for your workload.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Finding Care Fast: An R Shiny App for Infectious Disease Exposure Response
2026-09-15.description: Local public health agencies must rapidly coordinate testing and vaccination for people who have been exposed to infectious diseases. At DeKalb Public Health, epidemiologists previously relied on manual Google Maps searches to identify the closest of four health centers for each patient. To address this complicated and time-consuming process, I developed an R Shiny app that ranks centers by driving distance using ZIP code centroids to preserve privacy. I utilized the openrouteserve API to calculate the distances and used the leaflet package to create interactive maps. The app supports single and batch address workflows, reduces coordination time, and demonstrates how open-source tools can have real-world impact in public health.

speakers.title: Consultant II, Guidehouse
speakers.description: Imari Genias is currently a Consultant II for Guidehouse. Previously, she was a Rollins Epidemiology Fellow at DeKalb Public Health in Decatur, GA. In this role, she contributed to data analysis, with a specialty in geospatial analysis and mapping. Imari holds a Master of Public Health (MPH) in Global Epidemiology from Emory University.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Keynote Sessions: Correct, reproducible, and transparent data agents (Sara & Simon), Building the Future of Data Science and AI with Posit and AWS (Jagjit Dhaliwal)
2026-09-15.description:
9 - 9:55am | How do we build competent data analysis agents? Data analysis requires a willingness to pause, question conclusions, dig into subtleties, and sit with uncertainty. Frontier LLMs, however, are optimized to push tasks toward completion rather than refraining from answering unanswerable questions. Drawing on our experience building data analysis agents, we'll share evaluations that expose where LLM-driven analysis goes wrong and design patterns that keep analyses correct, transparent, and reproducible.

speakers.title: Senior Software Engineer, Posit
speakers.description: Simon Couch builds tools that make the work of data science more joyful and effective. As an engineer on the AI Core Team at Posit, his work spans coding assistants, model evaluations, and next-edit-suggestion systems. Drawing on his background in statistics, Simon spent several years authoring and maintaining packages in the open-source tidymodels framework—like stacks, broom, and infer—before shifting his focus to LLMs. He blogs about his work at simonpcouch.com.

2026-09-15.sessionName: Positron for Everyone: Organization-Wide Posit Tooling on Amazon SageMaker
2026-09-15.description: Unlock the full potential of your analytics team by deploying Positron as a managed, organization-wide environment within Amazon SageMaker Studio. This joint session with Posit and AWS explores how to provide analysts with a browser-based, scalable IDE equipped with R, Python, and Quarto, all while maintaining seamless AWS integration. We will detail the analyst experience, including built-in AI assistance via Bedrock-powered Posit Assistant, and provide technical insights for platform teams on managing deployments, licensing, and security at scale. Eliminate local environment friction and empower your organization with a unified, cloud-native workspace.

speakers.title: Head of Partner Solutions Architect AI/ML, Data & Analytics, AWS

2026-09-15.sessionName: Lunch & Learn: Bridging R, Python, and Snowflake: AI-Assisted Workflows and Native MLOps with Positron
2026-09-15.description:
Join us for an interactive Lunch & Learn session demonstrating how Posit tools integrate with Snowflake’s data and AI capabilities to streamline full-lifecycle data science.

Part 1: AI-Assisted Development with Positron, Snowflake Skills, and Cortex LLMs. Experience the next generation of data science workflows inside Positron, Posit's polyglot IDE. We will demonstrate how Posit Assistant combines with custom Snowflake skills and Cortex LLMs to help you query data, write optimized code, and leverage secure, enterprise-grade AI models, all without leaving your development environment.

Part 2: End-to-End MLOps with snowflake-r and Snowflake's Model Registry. Take models from prototype to production using native R and Python tooling. We will walk through an end-to-end MLOps workflow leveraging the open-source snowflake-r community packages. Learn how to engineer features, train models, register versioned artifacts, and deploy them for scalable, in-database scoring, bringing your code directly to the data.

Part 3: Reporting: What Posit Connect can do for you. After creating a model, vibecode a Shiny frontend and deploy it to Connect with one click!

Whether you are looking to accelerate daily coding with integrated LLM assistants or establish robust, scalable MLOps pipelines across R and Python, this session offers practical patterns you can immediately apply to your team's stack.

Key Takeaways for Attendees

  • How to leverage Posit Assistant in Positron with tailored Snowflake skills and Cortex LLMs.
  • How to use snowflake-r packages to interact smoothly with Snowflake data pipelines.
  • Best practices for managing features and registering models with Posit and Snowflake

2026-09-15.sessionName: No bad vibes: Building agents you can trust
data-dict & data-diff: two tools supporting AI-human data science collaboration

2026-09-15.sessionName: The Shiny AI Stack: shinychat, querychat, and the LLM Plumbing Beneath
2026-09-15.description: LLM-powered chat is becoming a core pattern in modern Shiny apps, but building a good chat experience (i.e., streaming, history, file attachments, editing, cancellation, etc) — is harder than it looks. In this talk, we'll tour the Shiny AI stack: shinychat's new getting-started API, which gives you a polished chat UI with all of these niceties out of the box, and the lower-level plumbing beneath it (ellmer and chatlas) that handles the connection to the LLM. We'll also see how these building blocks power domain-specific applications like querychat, and why they're designed to be general enough for essentially any LLM-powered Shiny app. Examples in R, with Python equivalents available for everything we'll cover.

2026-09-15.sessionName: AI Agents for Data Science: Posit Assistant, Commons, and Beyond
2026-09-15.description:
Last year at posit::conf, we at Posit unveiled two new data science agents: Positron Assistant and Databot. Your feedback was loud and clear: having two Posit agents was confusing. So this year we’re back with three new Posit agents!

In all seriousness, last year’s two agents merged their strengths to become Posit Assistant, which is now available in both Positron and RStudio, on the desktop and in Posit Workbench, and supports lots of different LLM providers and models. I’ll explain why we think the design choices we made in Posit Assistant make it the best agent for both data work and for coding.

I’ll give you an up close look at Commons, which lets you create data-oriented AI agents for others in your organization to use, and includes our latest ideas for making data agents as trustworthy as possible, even for non-experts.

And finally, I’ll give you a sneak peek at [REDACTED], our most AI-forward data science tool yet.

2026-09-15.sessionName: AI Governance in Posit Team: getting trustworthy results from agentic helpers
2026-09-15.description: AI agents like Posit Assistant, pi, Claude Code, and Codex are here to stay. Ensuring the results you deliver are trustworthy when agents do some of the work can be daunting. In this talk, we’ll explore how Governance done well is not bureaucracy but is empowering for the individual as well as the organization, offer some useful definitions of Risk and Compliance, and take a tour through emerging governance capabilities including open source desktop agentic tools, Posit.AI Pass Zero Data Retention access to curated models, and upcoming Posit Team features for putting supervision and guardrails around your agents.

2026-09-14.sessionName: Getting Started with Positron: An AI-Ready Polyglot Workflow for Data Science
2026-09-14.description:
This virtual three hour workshop provides a quick start for R and Python users who are curious about Positron, Posit’s new AI-ready polyglot code editor for data science. Here, you will learn how to use Positron’s time saving features to do a typical end-to-end data science task. Along the way, you will learn how to:

  • Install packages and set up a reproducible environment
  • Connect to a database
  • Add Positron Extensions 
  • Navigate the Command Palette
  • Configure Positron to use your favorite LLM model provider
  • Write, Edit, and Debug code with Positron’s built in AI Client
  • Use an LLM to explain and translate code
  • Learn the best practices for cleaning and exploring data with LLMs
  • Publish APIs, docs, apps and more with the Posit Publisher extension

This workshop will be a good fit for you as long as you have a basic familiarity with at least one of R or Python. No installation is necessary. Posit will provide a cloud environment equipped with both Positron and the LLMs we will use during class.

2026-09-14.sessionName: Administering and Orchestrating Next-Gen Statistical Environments for AI and Open Source Enabled Infrastructure for Regulated Use Cases
2026-09-14.description: This workshop will explore practical approaches to building reproducible, well-governed R environments for regulated pharmaceutical work. We will discuss package management, risk-based package validation, deployment options such as containers and managed platforms, and the controls needed to support traceability, change management, and production readiness. Through interactive discussion, participants will consider what a minimum viable approach looks like for administering R environments across research, development, and GxP use cases. We’ll also look at the impact of AI on regulated environments.

speakers.title: Manager Platform Engineer, Pfizer Inc.
speakers.description:
Casey Johnson is a Platform Manager at Pfizer, where he oversees the strategic direction and operational excellence of the enterprise data science platforms for Posit. With nearly 10 years of experience, Casey ensures the stability, scalability, and high performance of Pfizer’s Posit Workbench, Connect and Package Manager environments, enabling researchers and data scientists to deploy applications and execute complex analyses seamlessly.

With a strong background in systems engineering and enterprise architecture, Casey specializes in navigating the intricacies of large-scale computational environments. His work focuses on proactively managing upgrade pathways, optimizing R and Python package dependency management, and designing robust, secure infrastructure. By aligning corporate IT standards with agile data science workflows, Casey helps maintain a reliable foundation that empowers Pfizer’s teams to focus on delivering life-changing scientific breakthroughs.

Casey enjoys collaborating with peers on best practices for scaling open-source tools in highly regulated spaces. Outside of platform architecture, Casey is an enthusiast of emerging technologies and enjoys practicing Brazilian Jiu Jitsu.

speakers.title: Principal Solutions Engineer, Posit
speakers.description: Michael Mayer is a Solutions Engineer at Posit. A scientist by training, he holds a PhD in theoretical astrophysics from the University of Heidelberg, Germany, then gradually went into IT to eventually become a specialist in high performance / scientific computing and a subject-matter expert for customers in the pharmaceutical industry.

speakers.title: Senior Director, Statistical Data Science Analytics, Pfizer
speakers.description: Mike K Smith is a Senior Director, Statistical Data Science Analytics at Pfizer where he has worked for over 30 years. He is also the current Chair of the R Consortium Board. Mike has had responsibility for looking after Pfizer’s R installations for about 15 years - he partners with his colleagues in the Digital IT department to deliver and continue to refine the production R release process. Mike leads the R Centre of Excellence at Pfizer where there are over 1000 colleagues (and growing!) within the R community. He’s an active member of the Posit Data Science Hangout and describes himself as a “Professional Geek”. In his spare time he’s also a geek, producing generative ambient music using Ableton Live.

speakers.title: Principal Data Scientist, Denali Therapeutics
speakers.description: Nicole Jones is a Principal Data Scientist at Denali Therapeutics, where she is the data science program lead the company's molecule to treat MPS IIIA, a pediatric rare disease. As data science program lead, she oversees all clinical trials related to the molecule and leads the data science team responsible for generating SDTM, ADaMs, and TLFs for clinical reporting needs, primarily using R. She holds a Master of Public Health in Epidemiology and Applied Biostatistics and has spent six years in the pharma/biotech industry. In addition to her role as data science program lead, she serves as an R package validation lead, helping ensure the quality of the R packages used for regulatory submissions. Nicole is passionate about applying data science and leveraging open-source tools to accelerate therapies and brings a practical, cross-functional perspective on the challenges of turning complex biological data into actionable insight.

speakers.title: Sr. Technical Platform Manager, Johnson & Johnson
speakers.description: Satish Murthy is a Senior Manager at Johnson & Johnson R&D-IT. He leads the Scientific Computing Platform, and has primary responsibility for supporting High-Performance Computing to support JNJ scientists in the area of Statistical Simulation Modeling, Clinical Trials, Peptide Design, Finite Element analysis and Computational Chemistry. He plays a crucial role in building solutions and platforms focusing on creating validated environments for reproducibility, ensuring that clinical studies and other research activities can be reliably replicated. Satish’s current capabilities include data analytics, reliability engineering, and the implementation of environments to enhance repeatability and reproducibility in pharmaceutical research. His expertise has been instrumental in advancing R&D capabilities, leveraging technology to improve patient outcomes, and streamline research processes.

2026-09-14.sessionName: AI-Powered Clinical Reporting in R with the Pharmaverse
2026-09-14.description: Modern clinical reporting workflows are evolving fast, and this workshop helps you keep pace with a practical, end-to-end approach in R. You’ll learn how to move from raw data to analysis deliverables using Pharmaverse tools, including standards-aligned SDTM preparation, efficient creation of ADaM datasets, and generation of high-quality tables, listings, and graphs (TLGs) supported by Analysis Results Datasets (ARDs). You’ll also see where AI-assisted tooling can fit naturally into the workflow to support faster iteration and reduce manual rework, without sacrificing transparency, reproducibility, or reviewability. Leave with a modular, reusable playbook for applying R to every stage of clinical reporting across your team.

speakers.title: Data Scientist, GSK
speakers.description: Becca Krouse is a data scientist in GSK’s Statistics and Data Science Innovation Hub where she focuses on enabling users across R&D. A biostatistician by training, she has experience spanning over 15 years in the field of clinical research and specializes in developing R-based tools.

speakers.title: Senior Manager, Statistical Data Scientist, Praxis Precision Medicines
speakers.description: Ben Straub is a Senior Manager Statistical Data Scientist at Praxis Precision Medicines. He has worked in the industry for 8 years and is always actively involved with internal and external initiatives around R Adoption activities for Clinical Reporting and beyond. Ben is actively helping to develop and maintain an end-to-end R package pipeline [(pharmaverse)](https://pharmaverse.org/) that addresses all the needs of Clinical Reporting with many awesome companies and individuals.  He is very excited for the future of using R and open source within Pharma.

speakers.title: Executive Director, Data Science and Clinical Data Analytics, Kardigan
speakers.description: Daniel D. Sjoberg (he/him) is the Visual Analytics Lead at Genentech. Previously, he was a Lead Data Science Manager at the Prostate Cancer Clinical Trials Consortium, and a Senior Biostatistician at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City. He enjoys R package development, creating many packages available on CRAN, R-Universe, and GitHub. He’s a co-organizer of rainbowR (a community that supports, promotes and connects LGBTQ+ people who code in the R language) and of the R Medicine Conference. Daniel is the winner of the 2024 R in Pharma Brian Bole Award of Excellence and the 2021 American Statistical Association (ASA) Innovation in Statistical Programming and Analytics award.

speakers.title: Senior Real-Time Visual Analytics Specialist, Roche
speakers.description: Magdalena Krochmal is a Senior Real-time Visual Analytics Specialist at Roche in Basel. Combining a Ph.D. in Bioinformatics with over a decade of experience, she focuses on the intersection of R development and user-centric design. In her current role, Magdalena specializes in building intuitive medical data review tools using R, Shiny, and the Teal framework. From automating SDTM workflows to creating interactive visualizations, Magdalena is dedicated to streamlining clinical submissions through rapid prototyping and data-driven innovation.

2026-09-14.description:
As the data science landscape evolves, many practitioners are looking to expand their toolkit to include Python. Led by Jeroen Janssens, author of the book Python Polars: The Definitive Guide and Rich Iannone, creator of the Great Tables package, this workshop will provide a practical, hands-on introduction to an end-to-end Python workflow.

We will move beyond the basics of syntax to focus on a modern stack that prioritizes readability and performance. Using Positron as our development environment, we’ll navigate a complete project lifecycle. The workshop covers:

  • Data Manipulation: performant data wrangling using Polars.
  • Visualization: implementing the Grammar of Graphics in Python with Plotnine.
  • Reporting: creating presentation-ready tables with Great Tables.
  • Modeling: building machine learning models using Scikit-Learn.

The workshop is structured around a single case study. You’ll work through a series of exercises designed to help you get familiar with these tools. By the end of the day, you’ll have a good idea of how to translate your data science skills into a Python context and a repository of code examples to apply to future projects. 

This workshop is a great fit for those getting started with data science as well as R users who want to get their feet wet with Python for doing data science.

speakers.title: Senior Software Engineer, Posit, PBC
speakers.description: Building the Positron IDE and various Python packages.

speakers.title: Head of Developer Relations, Posit
speakers.description: Jeroen Janssens, PhD, is Head of Developer Relations at Posit, PBC. His expertise lies in visualizing data, implementing machine learning models, and building solutions using Python, R, JavaScript, and Bash. He’s passionate about open source and sharing knowledge. He’s the author of Python Polars: The Definitive Guide (O’Reilly, 2025) and Data Science at the Command Line (O’Reilly, 2021). Jeroen holds a PhD in machine learning from Tilburg University and an MSc in artificial intelligence from Maastricht University. He lives with his wife and two kids in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.

speakers.title: Software Engineer, Posit, PBC
speakers.description: Richard Iannone is a software engineer at Posit, PBC. He focuses on building open-source tools that help people work more effectively with data. In R, he works on several packages including gt, pointblank, and blastula. In Python, his focus is on Great Tables (a port of gt) and Great Docs (documentation-site generator for Python libraries).

2026-09-14.sessionName: Our Modern R Workflow (ft. Positron and AI)
2026-09-14.description:
This workshop is designed for data scientists who are comfortable with using R for data analysis and ready to level up their software engineering skills. Led by Hadley Wickham and Jenny Bryan, you’ll learn how to write more robust, maintainable R code while taking advantage of modern tooling (cough AI cough) that can dramatically accelerate your productivity.

We’ll cover three interconnected themes. First, you’ll learn contemporary R development practices—writing functions, organizing code into packages, testing, and documentation strategies that scale from personal projects to team collaboration. Second, we’ll explore how AI assistants like Claude Code can help you write better R code faster. Third, we’ll share practical tips for getting the most out of Positron, including features specifically designed to make R development and data exploration more fluid.

Throughout the workshop, we’ll emphasize the connections between these topics: how good development practices make AI assistance more effective, how modern tooling reduces friction so you can focus on the interesting problems, and how to build workflows that are both efficient and reproducible. You’ll leave with concrete skills you can apply immediately to your own projects.

Prerequisites: Basic familiarity with R programming (e.g. using the tidyverse). You should have written a few functions before, but don’t need any experience with package development, AI coding tools, or Positron. If you have taken a package development workshop before, you’ll learn what’s changed in our workflows, especially how we’re using AI and Positron effectively.

Learn how to successfully develop Machine Learning using R. tidymodels is a complete framework that implements modeling best practices using tidyverse principles. The tidymodels framework is a collection of packages for modeling and machine learning using tidyverse principles. 

Led by Max Kuhn and Emil Hvitfeldt, this workshop will teach you core tidymodels packages to preprocess data, specify and train models, and optimize the tuning parameter. You’ll learn tidymodels syntax as well as the process of predictive modeling for tabular data. Time permitting, you’ll be introduced to basic pre-processing with recipes.

This workshop is for you if you:

  • Are comfortable using tidyverse packages to read data into R, transform and reshape data, and make a variety of graphs, and
  • Have some experience with modeling, such as linear regression, logistic regression, or tree-based models. 

While the workshop will teach some terminology and modeling philosophy, it is primarily focused on showing users how to effectively develop, iterate, and validate a machine learning model.

speakers.title: Senior Software Engineer, Posit
speakers.description: Emil Hvitfeldt is a software engineer at Posit and part of the tidymodels team’s effort to improve R’s modeling capabilities. He maintains several packages within the realms of modeling, text analysis, and color palettes. Trying to make slidecrafting a well respecting verb. He co-authored the book Supervised Machine Learning for Text Analysis in R with Julia Silge. Working on book Feature Engineering A-Z.

2026-09-14.sessionName: Practical Quarto: Patterns, Templates, and Tooling
2026-09-14.description:
This workshop is designed for Quarto users who want to update and extend their Quarto mastery. Led by Charlotte Wickham and Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, this workshop will introduce new features of Quarto as well as blend practical recipes with conceptual understanding, so you can both copy–paste what works and understand why it works. Rather than a linear tour of Quarto features, the workshop is organized as a collection of focused, reusable patterns—each one solving a real authoring or publishing problem you’re likely to encounter.

Themes will include:

  • Design once, use anywhere: Learn how to work effectively with light and dark modes, brands, and renderings, and how to share a consistent brand across multiple Quarto projects without duplication or fragility.
  • Build reusable structures: Use template partials to factor out repeated content and layouts, making large or long-lived projects easier to maintain and evolve.
  • Understand why Typst matters: Explore why Typst deserves a place on your radar, with concrete “quick wins” that show how it can dramatically simplify PDF generation.
  • Work productively in Positron: Pick up Positron- and Quarto-specific productivity tips, including auto-formatting with Air, and practical ways to incorporate LLMs into your Quarto workflow.
  • Master freezing and reproducibility: Demystify freeze—when to check it in to version control, when to refresh it, and how to use it intentionally to balance reproducibility, performance, and collaboration.

By the end of the workshop, you’ll have a curated set of Quarto recipes and a mental model for how the pieces fit together. You’ll leave the workshop equipped to create more polished documents, scale your workflows across projects and teams, and make deliberate, informed choices about tools, formats, and authoring strategies.

2026-09-14.sessionName: Programming with LLMs in R and Python
2026-09-14.description:
Large Language Models (LLMs) offer developers unprecedented programmatic capabilities. Led by Garrick Aden-Buie and Sara Altman, this workshop will introduce ellmer (R) and chatlas (Python), Posit packages that simplify LLM API integration, handling conversation complexities and enabling seamless interactions with AI models. You’ll gain a conceptual understanding of both ecosystems, but you can choose your own adventure (R or Python) for hands-on coding sessions. 

Participants will explore system prompt design, token management, and tool calling while building familiarity with current AI technologies. The workshop demonstrates that:

  • Coding with LLMs unlocks possibilities beyond standard tools
  • No advanced AI background is required
  • Implementing AI can be both accessible and exciting

Designed for AI newcomers and experienced developers, the session covers LLM integration, Shiny web app development, and touches on advanced topics like dynamic information retrieval, context engineering, and agentic workflows. Attendees will gain hands-on experience through guided exercises, providing the confidence to start their LLM journey. As a dual-language workshop, attendees can choose hands-on practice in R or Python.

speakers.title: Senior Developer Advocate, Posit
speakers.description: Sara Altman is a developer advocate on the AI Core team at Posit, where she focuses on how AI can be effectively and thoughtfully used for data science. She co-authors the Posit AI newsletter with Simon Couch. Previously, she helped build Posit Academy and taught data science and R at Stanford.

2026-09-14.sessionName: Getting Started with Positron: An AI-Ready Polyglot Workflow for Data Science
2026-09-14.description:
This virtual three hour workshop provides a quick start for R and Python users who are curious about Positron, Posit’s new AI-ready polyglot code editor for data science. Here, you will learn how to use Positron’s time saving features to do a typical end-to-end data science task. Along the way, you will learn how to:

  • Install packages and set up a reproducible environment
  • Connect to a database
  • Add Positron Extensions 
  • Navigate the Command Palette
  • Configure Positron to use your favorite LLM model provider
  • Write, Edit, and Debug code with Positron’s built in AI Client
  • Use an LLM to explain and translate code
  • Learn the best practices for cleaning and exploring data with LLMs
  • Publish APIs, docs, apps and more with the Posit Publisher extension
