This workshop will be a good fit for you as long as you have a basic familiarity with at least one of R or Python. No installation is necessary. Posit will provide a cloud environment equipped with both Positron and the LLMs we will use during class.

This virtual session will have 4 20-minute talks!

  • AI/ML SOS IDK | Olivia Hebner and Kathryn Cronquist | Summit
    Many data scientists working in R are comfortable with regression but feel overwhelmed when getting started with machine learning. Often the challenge isn’t the algorithms, it’s knowing how to structure a clean, reproducible workflow. In this session, we’ll provide a beginner-friendly on-ramp to machine learning using tidymodels within Posit tools. Through a simple random forest example, we’ll demonstrate how data splitting, preprocessing, model specification, and evaluation fit together. Attendees will leave with a clear starting framework they can immediately apply to their own ML projects in R.
  • Nowcasting Pertussis Case Counts in Washington State | Allie Warren | Washington State Department of Health
    Pertussis is a highly contagious respiratory infection, but pertussis surveillance can lag by weeks due to delays between symptom onset and reporting and the need for case investigations, limiting timely outbreak response. Nowcasting—forecasting the present from incomplete data—addresses this gap by estimating the final case count for a given onset date. At the Washington State Department of Health, we implemented a process to track the pertussis reporting delays and used the epinowcast R package to model current pertussis case counts. Nowcasting reduced the timeframe from 9 weeks for complete data to 2 weeks for reliable estimates, improving real-time awareness of pertussis trends, which allows for earlier interventions during outbreaks.
  • Beyond Prediction: A Causal Framework using R for solving real world problems | Kimberley Isabel Orozco Cornejo | ixpantia
    Standard machine learning excels at prediction, but often fails to answer strategic questions like: "What caused this?" or "What if we intervened?". Stakeholders need causal answers, not just correlations. In "Beyond Prediction, A Causal Framework using R for solving real world problems" we'll tackle a churn scenario where predictive models give wrong advice due to Simpson's Paradox. I will demonstrate how to build a reproducible causal framework in R. Using dagitty to map assumptions and other R packages to orchestrate data simulation, attendees will learn to build an in silico laboratory. People will leave knowing how to disentangle true effects from spurious correlations to drive reliable decision-making using R.
  • Interpretable NLP for Clinical Imaging: Using tidymodels and Lasso-Regularized Text Models to Classify Pleural Effusion Impressions in R | Kaitlyn Housel | University of Pennsylvania
    Clinical imaging reports contain critical diagnostic information, but their free-text format limits large-scale analysis. This talk presents an interpretable NLP pipeline built in R using tidymodels and lasso-regularized logistic regression to classify radiology impressions for pleural effusion. To improve clinical usefulness, I developed complementary functions that extract structured signals for effusion size and loculations, reducing ambiguity and strengthening model performance. The workflow emphasizes reproducibility and auditability, combining sparse text features with domain feature engineering. Attendees will learn a practical approach for modeling clinical text and strategies for augmenting statistical models with rule-based logic.

speakers.title: Clinical Data Specialist, University of Pennsylvania
speakers.description:
Kaitlyn is a clinical data professional with a decade-long career arc spanning athletic training, clinical research coordination, and applied data science in academic medical settings. She currently works as a Data Coordinator in the Neonatology division at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), where she focuses on leveraging structured and unstructured EHR data to support pediatric clinical quality improvement. 

Kaitlyn also serves as a clinical data specialist at the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, where she built and maintained reproducible data pipelines in R, managed clinical trial data, and developed natural language processing workflows for extracting clinical meaning from free-text EHR data. Her deep clinical background shapes how she approaches data problems, grounding computational methods in the realities of how clinicians document and how care is delivered. Kaitlyn is passionate about the intersection of clinical expertise and data science.

She holds an MS in Athletic Training, a Data Analytics Certification from the University of Pennsylvania and completed CHOP's Data and Analytics University fellowship. Her work has contributed to publications in critical care and concussion research.

speakers.title: Data Science and Methodology Lead, ixpantia

2026-09-14.description:
There are 3 20-minute talks in this session!

  • Let Your LLM Surprise You: Inbox Insights with ellmer and Posit Connect | Konstantinos Ntentes | Posit
    What if your team received a fresh, data-backed marketing insight every morning—without anyone writing it? In this talk, I’ll walk through how ellmer connects our enterprise LLM to sales-and-marketing funnel views, and how Posit Connect and blastula turn that output into actionable, inbox-ready insights with a supporting gt table and reproducible code chunk. I’ll also share how we balance analysis guardrails with creative freedom, maintain variety across runs, why misses are still useful, and how this work fits into our team’s roadmap toward trustworthy natural-language access to complex analytics for non-coder stakeholders.
  • An R app for generating appraisals reports | Michael Morales | INTUS
    Where I work, one of the teams used to write property appraisal reports in a spreadsheet. Each one had to do the edition, formatting, calculations, pictures, in a file saved locally in their computers.
    We wanted to design an app that helped them to create the report, to just enter the parameters and pictures, and let the program do the formatting, the calculations, download the report, and saving the information into the cloud facilitating the data extraction.
    And this is how we came out with PAO, which can be translated as Platform for appraisals Online, an app written in R via shinyapps, that uses officeR, flextable, bslib, etc, connects to AWS’ S3 and RDS, to save pictures and data into databases, facilitating their daily work.
  • Positron Notebooks: Built Around How You Actually Work | Nick Strayer | Posit
    At this conference you will find no shortage of presentations on what Positron does, but I want to focus on the why of the Positron Notebook Editor. We talked to data scientists across a variety of data science teams about how they work in notebooks day to day. Those conversations shaped how we built the Positron Notebook Editor.
    The goal is the feeling you loved in RStudio, where everything you need is right at your fingertips, extended into notebooks: the features you need where they feel natural. IDE features like the interactive data explorer and kernel-aware AI assistant live right inside your notebook workflow. We'll demo the full loop live: exploring data, visualizing it, and sharing results out to stakeholders.

speakers.title: Senior Data Analyst, Intus
speakers.description: A mathematician that have joy in solving different problems for different areas within the company by using all available tools, specially if it can transform into a shinyapps solution.

2026-09-14.description:
This virtual session will have 4 20-minute talks!

  • I Didn't Abandon R—I Added Python: My Story of Growing Without Starting Over | Bilikisu Wunmi Olatunji | R-Ladies Global/ R-Ladies Abuja
    I built my consulting career with R. It helped me deliver analyses, dashboards, reports, and models that clients trusted. Then I started seeing opportunities that were a perfect fit for my experience—but they expected Python. Like many people, I told myself I wasn't ready.
    This talk is the story of how I stopped letting a programming language define my professional identity and started building on what I already knew. Through a real consulting project—not a code walkthrough—I’ll share the practical playbook that helped me transition confidently: Wrap → Validate → Swap. Along the way, I'll show how lightweight metric contracts and golden datasets helped me keep results consistent while working across R and Python.
    You'll leave with practical ideas for expanding your opportunities, navigating mixed-language environments with confidence, and growing your career without feeling like you have to start over.
  • Combining Agentic Python Applications with R Workflows Using Posit Connect | Luis Wirth | HMS Analytical Software
    Companies rely on R for their analytical workflows, while Python now supports agentic LLM-based systems, motivating architectures that combine both ecosystems.
    This talk presents a system where a Python application acts as a frontend and an agentic orchestrator and delegates code execution to an R backend. Both applications are deployed on Posit Connect via an automatic git deployment workflow. The apps communicate via API calls, allowing the agent to trigger R-based tasks such as data wrangling, plotting, and statistical calculations. Using a real system with demo data, we focus on presenting architecture and deployment patterns and discuss benefits and tradeoffs compared to all-Python or all-R designs.
  • Shift-left for more accessibility | Björn Fisseler | FernUniversität in Hagen
    Quarto lets authors produce reports, slides, and dashboards from plain-text source files, but these outputs aren’t accessible by default. This talk presents practical workflows, tools, and design guidelines to build accessible Quarto content from the start. I cover the POUR principles, semantic document structure, accessible tables and figures, alt-text strategies for plots, and comparisons of R packages and AI-assisted approaches for generating descriptions. Attendees will leave with a checklist, examples, and methods for manual and automated accessibility testing to integrate into reproducible workflows.
  • Where Do Notebooks Come From? | Wasim Lorgat | Posit
    Quarto and Jupyter are two of the most widely used tools in computational notebooks, but they offer very different experiences. Why is that?
    This talk traces two threads of development that led to where we are today, from Donald Knuth's vision of writing code as narrative, a tradition that eventually led to Quarto, as well as John McCarthy's interactive LISP paradigm whose legacy inspired the scientific Python tools that led to Jupyter.
    These threads are now converging, with the Positron IDE at the intersection, bringing the literate program and the interactive notebook together in one environment.
    I hope this talk gives you a new way to think about the tools you use every day, and the confidence to try the ones you don't.

speakers.title: Senior AI Engineer, HMS Analytical Software GmbH

2026-09-16.sessionName: Do This Instead: 4 Alternatives to Common Charts
2026-09-16.description:
Even in “good” charts, it’s easy to miss or misinterpret key patterns in the data. Common best practices — continuous color scales, equally spaced gridlines, month-level aggregation, etc — leave critical leaps from numbers to meaning up to visual perception and unexamined assumptions.

“Do This Instead” offers 5 specific before/after replacements for common analysis situations. For example, grouping continuous values into meaningful categories lets us use facet_wrap to create small multiples instead of relying on color perception. And, explicitly defining what counts as “high” creates a shared, expertise-grounded interpretation. 

Techniques are tool-agnostic; examples implemented in ggplot.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

speakers.title: Independant Data Viz Specialist
speakers.description: Zan creates charts and graphs which change how people look at their data (literally). Her focus on data viz for analysis leads to better decision making, data driven questions, deeper understanding, and new discoveries.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Quack to the Future: Building Traceable Data Lakehouses with DuckLake in R
2026-09-16.description: Modern data pipelines need more than clean outputs: they need a paper trail. This talk introduces two R packages to help you build a lakehouse stack using DuckLake for transactional storage and dplyneage for column-level lineage tracking. We'll walk through a medallion architecture (bronze → silver → gold) built with dplyr familiar workflows, where every table write is versioned with author and commit message. You'll see how to visualize lineage flows across pipeline layers, time-travel back to earlier table versions, and audit exactly how your data changed and why, all without leaving R.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Building a Custom Version of GeoGuessr in R
2026-09-16.description: This is about using R creatively for non-traditional tasks, with an example of building a custom version of the game GeoGuessr in R. Attendees at this session will learn not only about the tools to build this, but how to innovatively solve problems in R. The process starts by taking a non-technical idea: a version of GeoGuessr just for New York City. Then breaking it down into smaller parts that R can handle: developing a Shiny dashboard frontend for players to interact with, encoding gameplay into data structures in Google Sheets for easy access for players, and building a backend to collect and process data from APIs. Attendees can play the live game with locations from the host city, Houston, to see R powering real-time gameplay.

2026-09-16.sessionName: ORCA: a collaboratively-built AI-powered Shiny app built on Posit Team
2026-09-16.description: ORCA is KS&R’s internal Shiny application for AI-assisted coding of open-ended survey responses. Designed in concert with Ketchbrook Analytics, ORCA combines an intuitive front-end for job submission, response review, and code editing with a modular backend built on the Posit ecosystem. The system integrates a {golem}-based Shiny app, a plumber API for asynchronous processing, pins for versioned metadata, and scheduled batch workflows for logging and delivery. This talk showcases how thoughtful UI/UX design and Posit-based infrastructure work together to operationalize AI in a transparent, reproducible research environment.

speakers.title: AI Engineer, CHG Healthcare
speakers.description:
I build AI-powered tools and data systems that solve real problems - production things that people actually use, not prototypes.

My background is unusual: a decade in academic research (PhD, 750+ citations) gave me rigorous experimental and analytical training, and the last several years have been spent applying that to full-stack AI and data engineering. I've shipped chatbots, automation pipelines, interactive dashboards, and internal platforms across market research, environmental consulting, and government sectors - working with everyone from Fortune 500 companies to federal agencies.

My technical core is R, Python, and JavaScript, with deep experience in Shiny, APIs and deployment infrastructure. I care about documentation, reproducibility, and knowledge transfer as much as shipping features.

I present at Posit::conf and similar venues. I mentor junior developers. I'm as comfortable whiteboarding architecture as I am writing the code.

I'm drawn to challenges at the intersection of AI engineering and data science, places where the problems are hard and the team wants to build things right.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Reusing 'ggplot2' code: how to design better plot helper functions
2026-09-16.description: Creating 'ggplot2' helper functions can help avoid repeatedly copying and pasting long and complex 'ggplot2' code chunks. However, if helper functions are not carefully designed, the initial convenience can often turn into frustration. While helper functions can reduce the amount of code needed to remake a complicated plot, they often mask the underlying layered grammar of graphics, complicating further customisation and tweaking of the plot. This talk addresses how to design effective 'ggplot2' plot helper functions that maximise reuse convenience whilst preserving access to the elegant flexibility of layered plot composition.

speakers.title: Post-Doctoral Researcher, LMU Munich
speakers.description: Cynthia Huang is a Post-Doctoral Research Fellow at LMU Munich. Her research focuses on formalisations and frameworks for leveraging generative AI and LLMs for data preparation and data visualisation. She is particularly interested how to harness and validate human-AI collaboration in exploratory data analysis, and ensuring trustworthy and interpretable data science when leveraging AI-assistance.

2026-09-16.sessionName: From Dplyr to Polars: Migrating Tools & Languages While Maintaining the Tidy Model
2026-09-16.description: Many data practitioners who learned analysis through R’s dplyr, discover that moving to Python can feel like losing a native language. I certainly felt that way, and my colleagues tend to echo the same sentiments. Learning new syntax is easy, but porting the mental model the tidyverse provides was the real challenge. In this talk I describe my personal migration from dplyr to Polars and how I rebuilt the mental model in a new ecosystem. I draw on my personal opinions and experience, the thoughts of colleagues, and the objective differences in technical goals and specifications. The goal of this talk is to show data practitioners how to preserve the workflows they loved in dplyr with the execution model of polars in python.

2026-09-16.sessionName: From internal scripts to public portfolios: building an open source program at Dow
2026-09-16.description: Dow's Citizen Data Science community is putting R and Python into the hands of chemical researchers across the company. As these data science workflows matured, we saw an opportunity: share our general-purpose tools with the broader community through an open source release program. This talk walks through how we built that program -- the policy, the legal review process, the release checklist -- and piloted it with six R packages for statistical analysis and experimental design. Attendees will leave with a practical playbook for standing up an open source release program at organizations where one doesn't yet exist.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Life after R4DS: How to take your R skills to the next level
2026-09-16.description:
Picture this: You've taken that difficult first step into learning R, and you've worked your way through a course, workshop, or online textbook like "R for Data Science". Your foundation is solid - but now what?

This talk will give you the resources you need to take your R skills to the next level. First, I will discuss the three ABCs of pathways forward to Intermediate R: Analysis of complex data, Building professional deliverables, and Coding/programming.

Then, I will share a new public course site designed for both classroom use and for self-guided learners. The course takes a "learn by doing" approach, with modular tracks structured around project that is completed progressively through hands-on exercises.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Cairn: From notebooks to logbooks
2026-09-16.description: Notebooks let you rewrite history. Logbooks don't. In logbook-mode analysis, history is a first-class citizen: cells, commentary, and AI exchanges are only ever appended so that the document becomes a chronological record of every step performed in a data analysis. I'll show why notebook software doesn't fully accommodate this style, and introduce Cairn, my attempt at supporting it properly: a Neovim plugin for stacking your analysis one stone at a time.

speakers.title: Senior Data Engineer, Juul Labs
speakers.description: Eric is a data engineer, analyst, and scientist with over a decade of experience spanning hardware, mobile apps, cryptocurrency, and commercial strategy.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Positron Everywhere All At Once
2026-09-16.description:
A modern data science IDE has to feel the same wherever someone opens it. Data scientists move constantly between personal laptops, shared servers, containerized workflows, and the mix of cloud and on-prem environments that shape day-to-day work. The tools they rely on need to travel with them.

Positron, a next-generation data science IDE, is one of those tools. Deploying it means meeting people on the platforms they already use. In this talk, I'll share strategies for bringing Positron to academic settings, where instructors and students juggle personal machines, course JupyterHub deployments, and department servers. I'll walk through real examples of running Positron Server through JupyterHub via jupyter-server-proxy, configuring it for classroom use, and weighing the tradeoffs of each approach. You'll leave with practical techniques for common academic deployment scenarios and a clearer sense of where Positron fits today.

speakers.title: Senior Software Engineer, Posit, PBC
speakers.description: Building the Positron IDE and various Python packages.

2026-09-16.sessionName: From ABC to AI: Applying Language Acquisition to R and Technical Mastery
2026-09-16.description:
The world’s most spoken language isn’t Python. It is English. As a second language learner who struggled before later teaching English and authoring a book on R, I learned that fluency comes from internalizing structure. 

In the age of AI, if models can generate code instantly, does learning R still matter? 

This talk introduces a Three Layer Model of Technical Mastery: 

Syntax, the vocabulary that AI accelerates; 
Structure, the grammar of tidyverse, Quarto, and Shiny workflows; 
Thinking, the human skills of framing problems and making judgments.

By mapping language learning to the evolution of a data scientist, this talk offers a practical framework for building durable skills in an AI assisted world.

2026-09-16.sessionName: How Shiny changed data analysis at the Metabolism Center
2026-09-16.description: Scientists in metabolic research increasingly rely on technologies measuring thousands of targets simultaneously, but many are still limited to analyses in spreadsheets Introducing Shiny transformed how our center works with data: an ecosystem of apps now gives researchers tools that once required coding, enabling faster exploration and richer insights. Data can be easily visualized with datasets from other researchers, allowing analysis in a broader context. Junior researchers are building new apps, sharing their analysis pipelines with the world. I will share some of our success stories, and highlight the packages we use to make apps fast, interactive, and intuitive.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Quarto Hub: Collaboratively edit, create, and share documents
2026-09-16.description: Quarto Hub is a new open-source and hosted platform from Posit. In Quarto Hub, you can create, edit, comment on, and publish your Quarto projects (single documents, presentations, websites) collaboratively. In this talk, we will give an overview of how it works, and how Quarto Hub interacts with existing code-first practices and text-based workflows. We will show how the architecture of Quarto Hub allows a variety of use cases, including (if time permits) integration with RStudio, Positron, and Posit AI.

2026-09-16.sessionName: From, "Can you Just Make Us a Dashboard" to Enterprise Systems in R
2026-09-16.description: Over the past five years, Mayo Clinic’s Data Visualization Lab has grown from three statisticians building simple dashboards in R into an enterprise team delivering production Shiny systems that support real clinical and operational decision-making. This talk shares lessons learned from scaling open-source tools in a highly regulated healthcare environment, where data are siloed, workflows are complex, and trust matters. I’ll discuss how we moved from ad-hoc dashboards to governed, maintainable applications using R, Shiny, REDCap, and Posit Connect, and what it took organizationally to make the shift succeed. Attendees will leave with concrete patterns for building credibility and responsibly scaling R-based systems in high-stakes settings.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Instant Feedback, Robust Evals: Agentic AI Tutoring in R and Python
2026-09-16.description: What if every open source data science resource included practice coding problems with immediate feedback? I made blendtutor and blendtutor-py so educators can hand-craft coding lessons installed as an R package or Python module. Learners then get immediate agentic AI-powered feedback on their code. And we don’t have to just hope the LLMs provide useful pointers. These packages give scaffolding to create custom LLM evals for every lesson. No matter the learning goal, educators can create lessons where LLMs steer learners in a helpful direction. The best version of these packages involves co-evolution with the community. I’m excited to figure out together how this active learning can support other open source resources.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Taming Messes with AI
R Nerds
The Design of Everyday R Functions
2026-09-16.description:
You might think "design" only applies to physical objects or visual interfaces like Shiny apps. But as Don Norman noted in The Design of Everyday Things, "all artificial things are designed." If users struggle with your code, it's a design flaw, not human error. Fortunately, good design isn't just for designers.

In this talk, I'll show you how to make your R functions easier to use. You'll learn how to better signify what a function does, how to be forgiving when users are a bit sloppy, and how to clearly explain what to do when your code can't fix a problem for them. I'll also equip you to teach AI agents to follow these principles, making your R functions easier to use even if you're the only user.

2026-09-16.sessionName: When the data doesn’t fit the question
2026-09-16.description: As the largest public funder of biomedical research worldwide, the National Institutes of Health has a responsibility to track the impact of its funding. An important metric for impact is research publications; however, publication databases are used across the scientific community without consideration of their integrity. These publication databases were often created prior to the development of fair data practices; therefore assessment of their current data integrity is critical. I assessed the data integrity of these databases using R and the tidyverse. I developed techniques for defining limitations, identifying standards, and refining analysis to ensure these databases are reviewed with integrity and used to their fullest potential.

speakers.title: Data Scientist, National Institutes of Health
speakers.description:
Kelli Goggans is a Data Scientist at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), evaluating biomedical research policies and programs through quantitative and qualitative analysis. Her work centers on data integrity at scale — developing protocols to clean and reconcile large datasets, establishing internal database access with full documentation, and building dashboards that give leadership a trustworthy, data-driven view for decision-making.

Kelli holds a Ph.D. in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology from the University of Alabama at Birmingham, where she designed and led experimental studies requiring multi-factorial statistical analysis. That grounding in experimental rigor now informs her approach to building trustworthy data pipelines and reporting systems.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Environmental Stressors and Healthcare: How a Posit/R Powered Pipeline Reveals Environmental Drivers of Emergency Department Strain
2026-09-16.description: Extreme heat and poor air quality strain Emergency Department (ED) operations. We scaled a Baytown pilot across Houston Methodist (HM) and packaged it for Texas Medical Center (TMC) partners using an end-to-end Posit stack. We integrate Epic/Clarity with EPA Air Quality System and NOAA Climate Data Online, model ED counts with tidymodels, and build spatial visualizations of ED demand across the HM service area with environmental hazard/amenity overlays (refineries, green space). We deliver Quarto reports for managers and a Shiny dashboard for leaders. Protected Health Information stays in database; artifacts are versioned (pins), served (vetiver), orchestrated (targets), and hosted on-network. A template repo enables sharing across TMC.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Lowering Cesarean Rates  - Using Quarto to Create Scalable Performance Reports
2026-09-16.description: Cesarean births can be lifesaving, but overuse carries health risks and financial costs. At the Obstetrics Initiative, we partner with 65+ Michigan hospitals to reduce unnecessary cesareans and improve maternal care. As Analytics Manager, I lead the development of performance reports built on near real-time EHR data to monitor trends, identify opportunities, and guide targeted support. We rely on Quarto to power scalable reporting pipelines and custom, one-off analyses. In this talk, I’ll share practical tips for using Quarto to build impactful analytics tools your stakeholders will actually use—and value.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Operationalizing Quality: Building an ICU Dashboard at the VA with Shiny
2026-09-16.description:
In the high-stakes environment of the VA Critical Care Service Line, data silos often hinder rapid decision-making. We replaced static, retrospective reporting with a production-grade Shiny dashboard to track key quality metrics across the VA Pittsburgh Healthcare System.

This talk explores the journey of building an operational tool that connects directly to the VA Corporate Data Warehouse (CDW). I will demonstrate how we leverage R and SQL to visualize complex clinical data, democratize access for leadership, and navigate the unique security constraints of a federal IT environment. Attendees will learn strategies for moving from "metrics on a spreadsheet" to interactive, reproducible dashboards that drive real clinical change.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Flipping the Switch
2026-09-16.description: Open source adoption is widely discussed, yet few enterprises complete a full digital transformation using only open source tools and languages. GSK R&D flipped the switch, moving 3,000+ colleagues from proprietary stacks to an open source. This session explains how we built a leadership-ready cost, risk, and productivity model; secured executive sponsorship; and planned the migration in waves without disrupting research delivery. We will cover governance, training, internal champions, and metrics that kept teams productive, plus what we would do differently. Attendees will learn how to take small organizations and experiments to full enterprise digital transformation so they can make the case to their own leaders.

speakers.title: Director of Data Science, GSK
speakers.description: I like R and open source technologies with a strong interest in the use of R in Pharma.

2026-09-16.sessionName: CancerTrialsBR: Improving Access to Cancer Clinical Trials in Brazil with R, Shiny and Large Language Models
2026-09-16.description: A lack of timely, accessible information is a major barrier to cancer trial recruitment. We present CancerTrialsBR, a Shiny app. that combines R, Google Maps, and LLM to improve access to trial information in Brazil. A daily R pipeline retrieves data from ClinicalTrials.gov, uses LLM to generate Portuguese summaries and descriptors, and standardize facilities with Google Maps. This enriched database can be accessed through a Shiny app., and users interact to suggest status alterations which are validated before integration. This project has partnered with the Brazilian Society of Clinical Oncology since Nov. 2025 and had 4,030 visits from 220 Brazilian cities. User feedback resulted in 34/57 updated status incorporated in the database.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Shining Stars
Open Source Routing Analysis at Scale
2026-09-16.description: Routing analysis is critical for understanding access to government services. My colleagues and I researched how access to Social Security Administration offices might change if some offices were to close, which the federal government proposed last year. However, nationwide routing analysis presents challenges: Google Maps API is prohibitively expensive, and open source OSRM's online server is for demonstration only. In this talk, we'll share how we used R, bash, and Docker to deploy a local OSRM server for nationwide routing analysis, present our findings on office closures, and explain how we're leveraging this infrastructure to enable future research on service accessibility.

speakers.title: Open Source Routing Analysis at Scale, The Urban Institute
speakers.description: Gabriel Morrison is a senior data scientist on the Technology and Data Science team at the Urban Institute. His work focuses on researching and building tools to address equity-related issues in cities and counties, often with spatial data. Morrison holds a BA in geographical sciences and an MS in computational analysis and public policy from the University of Chicago.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Lowering Barriers to Learning
No Good Deed Goes Unscaled
Quarto, Connected
Quarto + Accessibility + You
2026-09-16.description:
New accessibility requirements from your organization might feel like a barrier between you and the tools you rely on. The irony? Accessibility is about removing barriers between your work and the people who need it. Fortunately, the landscape for Quarto users is rapidly improving.

In this talk, I'll share what's new in Quarto and related tools that make producing accessible documents easier than ever. You'll learn what you need to know as a Quarto user to ensure your work reaches everyone who needs it.

2026-09-16.sessionName: The Evolving Craft of Data Science
Can I offer you a nice IDE in this trying time?
2026-09-16.description: Adopting new tools means overcoming a learning curve, motivated by familiarity with added benefits or by new and worthwhile capabilities. This happens with IDE use in research and education, where RStudio can be synonymous with R itself. Since Positron's release as a multilingual data science IDE, experienced users quickly saw its potential, but many others remained hesitant. Missing RStudio features caused resistance, while capabilities like multiple R installations, fast exploration of large datasets, and spreadsheet extensions drove wider adoption. This talk highlights how incremental, user-centered improvements can lower the barriers to entry. Switching IDEs depends not just on novel features, but on addressing unspoken frustrations.

speakers.title: Biodiversity Scientist, Instituto de Ecología A.C. INECOL
speakers.description: Mammals, biodiversity, open science, R

2026-09-16.sessionName: Friends till the End(-to-end): Moving R and Python Projects into Pipelines with targets and Hamilton
2026-09-16.description:
Using R and Python within the same project liberates data scientists to work with whoever and whatever (software) they want. But moving these projects from notebooks into production can feel like picking a favorite child: which language should control the pipeline? 

I want to empower polyglot data scientists to face this choice head-on by sharing my experience building mixed language pipelines with R's 'targets' package and Python's 'Hamilton' package. Because these packages share similar, "functional" syntax to define pipelines, data scientists can use the same logic in both languages! I demonstrate the pros and cons of each choice by showing how I moved a ‘targets’ pipeline into ‘Hamilton’ to solve collaborative and technical challenges.

speakers.title: Legal Data Analyst, Consilio
speakers.description: Cory is a data scientist on a mission to bring reproducibility and transparency to the legal industry. He uses R and Python to build pipelines that analyze legal documents, eDiscovery workflows, and court decisions. When he isn’t busy replacing ad-hoc processes with code-first workflows, he’s usually hanging out with his three beloved cats.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Slideware Is Dead - Long Live Quarto
2026-09-16.description:
There have been, over the years, many reasons why one would use PowerPoint, Canva, and Keynote over Quarto for making slides.

Despite many of the core features from quarto, such as code results and humanly readable file formats, there are still some tactile elements that 
makes slideware favourable to the code-focused Quarto slides.

This will go over the changes in Quarto itself and the slide-specific features that make the experience of creating slides in Quarto just as nice as in any other software.

This includes, but is not limited to: allowing you to move and center images, add arrows, and fix typos directly in the slides.

speakers.title: Senior Software Engineer, Posit
speakers.description: Emil Hvitfeldt is a software engineer at Posit and part of the tidymodels team’s effort to improve R’s modeling capabilities. He maintains several packages within the realms of modeling, text analysis, and color palettes. Trying to make slidecrafting a well respecting verb. He co-authored the book Supervised Machine Learning for Text Analysis in R with Julia Silge. Working on book Feature Engineering A-Z.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Clinical data harmonization with LLMs
2026-09-16.description: Clinical trial data formats differ across studies and over time, even within an organization. After years of writing bespoke R code to harmonize data for cross-study analysis, my team is developing LLM-assisted automation. First, we use an LLM to develop a data model for the output, describing a format and content that accommodates all input studies. Then an LLM evaluates each study’s data files and documentation to determine how to wrangle each input file to fit the data model. The LLM generates yaml configuration files for programmatically transforming each study into an interoperable format for combined analysis. Our LLM prompts, data model, configuration files, and pipeline code are all version controlled and reproducible.

speakers.title: Senior Principal Data Scientist, Bristol Myers Squibb
speakers.description:
Leslie Emery, PhD, is a Senior Principal Data Scientist in the Knowledge Science Research team at Bristol Myers Squibb working on research for cancer treatments. She works with a team of translational data scientists to design and deploy innovative analysis-ready data products for exploratory research. These data products include custom data transformation, visualization, & quality tracking apps in R Shiny and curated & standardized data sets for analysis. She has particular expertise in harmonizing data from many disparate sources into combined data sets that enable cross-study or cross-disease analysis. Leslie works closely with stakeholders from Informatics & Predictive Sciences and Translational Medicine to define their data and visualization requirements and deliver them in elegant and efficient ways. Her work makes it easy for scientists doing drug development research to answer their scientific questions.

Leslie completed her PhD in genome sciences at the University of Washington studying the patterns that evolution and population history have left in current human genetic variation. She then worked as a Research Scientist at UW Biostatistics on NIH consortium projects identifying the genetic variants that contribute to common human diseases. She co-led a team that designed a reproducible python + R pipeline and SQL database for harmonizing health measurement data for the TOPMed whole genome sequencing project.

Leslie's many hobbies include knitting, crochet, reading sci-fi, and tracking and analyzing her hobby data.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Running a software department in times of agents
2026-09-16.description:
This abstract might be written by some LLM tool. The majority of the work we used to do is different right now. The challenges my team faces in February might be quite different in September.

I'm the Head of Technology at Appsilon, which means that I take care of around 40 R and Python devs across dozens of projects. My daily work is heavily affected by the AI revolution: I advise on the best tools, react to the expectations that "vibe-coding" will do the job, handle recruitment fraud attempts, and build complex-packages-specialized AI agents.

The audience will have the opportunity to hear my experiences on how AI works on scale, from the front-line perspective of a company for which leveraging AI properly is an existential challenge.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Pretty Useful Data Viz
The NASA Earthdata Cloud Cookbook: A Quarto Collaboration Story
2026-09-16.description: A shared problem can help unite people to work together for a common solution, which they can then adapt to address further needs. NASA Earthdata staff manage over 100 petabytes of data and create tutorials to help scientists access these data with code. Since 2021, Quarto has helped NASA Openscapes mentors solve a shared problem by being a place to unite and build tutorials together, creating a “Cookbook” of Python and R tutorials with less redundancy – and help establish open source practices across a government agency. We'll share how over 5 years of Cookbook collaboration and governance have shaped these mentors' workflows, letting them focus on what matters: helping scientists work with NASA Earthdata efficiently.

speakers.title: Openscapes
speakers.description: Andy Teucher is a core Openscapes team member and develops software and cloud infrastructure. He is a biologist turned data scientist and R developer, specializing in helping people and organizations build maintainable, reproducible data workflows. Andy is a strong open data and open code advocate, and believes in the value of using and contributing to open-source software.

2026-09-16.sessionName: From laptop to cluster
First Impressions Matter: Styling Data Products That People Actually Want to Use
2026-09-16.description: Professional styling isn't a luxury for data products—it determines whether users engage with our insights or click away. But for data scientists already managing complex code, mastering CSS to achieve polished results can feel overwhelming. This talk demonstrates how Bootswatch and brand.yml help you create professionally styled HTML-based products without CSS expertise. You'll learn to leverage ready-made themes with pick-and-choose YAML-based customization, taking your data products from functional-but-forgettable to professional and memorable tools people trust and rely on. Whether building internal dashboards or public-facing applications, you'll leave with practical examples and techniques to implement immediately.

speakers.title: Senior Health Research Analyst, The Ohio State University

2026-09-16.sessionName: Never Block, Never Copy: mirai + mori from Shiny to the Cluster
2026-09-16.description:
Most parallel R is batch-and-wait: send off your tasks, wait for the slowest — and you're locked out while it runs. In a Shiny app, every user freezes. There's a quieter cost: eight workers each need their own copy of your data, so a 200 MB data frame becomes 1.6 GB to serialize, move, and hold in RAM. Your laptop habits die at deployment.

This talk shows you how to fix both problems with two CRAN packages, mirai and mori, building a production-ready memory model for event-loop applications. mirai keeps the event loop moving: it processes results as they arrive instead of blocking, and it's first-class in Shiny. When many users show up at once,

mirai can put a hard cap on how much data waits in the queue. When that limit is reached, it hands back control to your app rather than freezing every session. mori, on the other hand, removes the pressure at source: put a dataset into shared memory once and every worker maps the same pages, so 200 MB per worker collapses to a 200-byte reference, with no changes to your downstream code.

The same app runs anywhere you have compute. A new HTTP launcher makes the cloud, Kubernetes, and Posit Workbench as easy to reach as your own servers over SSH or an HPC cluster through its scheduler, and moving between them takes a single line of configuration.

Scale further. Scale safely. Never block, never copy — from your Shiny app to your cluster.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Teach Once, Use Often: Building AI Skills for Data Analysis
2026-09-16.description: AI tools are increasingly part of the modern analyst's workflow—but generic prompting only gets you so far. Skills are structured prompts that teach an AI how to operate within a specific analytical context. In this talk, I'll walk through what skills are and why they matter, how to build one from scratch, and where to find community skills across Posit and other repositories. Along the way, I'll argue that developing a skill isn't just about configuring an AI—it's a valuable exercise in clarifying your own priorities, best practices, and standards for success. Rather than removing the analyst from the process, it can put them front and center. This talk will focus on the analyst and how they can use these tools to improve their work.

2026-09-16.sessionName: LLM-Powered Data Workflows: Structuring Inputs and Accelerating Insight
2026-09-16.description: As organizations scale, the bottleneck is rarely data availability — it’s operationalizing that data reliably. Automation demands structure, yet real-world inputs are inconsistent, and even clean datasets require time-consuming interpretation before decisions can be made. This session presents two production LLM-powered systems: one that semantically standardizes unpredictable raw datasets for downstream automation, and another that transforms structured survey data into executive-ready narratives and interactive insights. Together, they illustrate how LLMs can enable scalable, decision-ready data workflows across the lifecycle.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Clinical Data Science
Package Your Judgment, Keep Your Intent
2026-09-16.description: Judgment is the capacity; your creative process is its observable trace. Every conversation with your agent is exactly that — a trace. You're already sharing your expertise, every day, with an audience of one. The alternative: package your judgment, keep your intent. This talk shows what that means in practice. At the UN we packaged our methodological judgment as a portable kit: a Python package, an MCP server, and a skill set that turns a generic coding agent into an opinionated pair-analyst for self-service analytics. You'll leave with a simple framework for what to package and what to keep, a structural answer to 'won't this replace me?' (it doesn't), and two public-good reasons to share your judgment."

speakers.title: United Nations
speakers.description: Mirian Lima is a research methodologist working with economic development data — she packages methods for a living. At the UN Office of the Special Adviser on Africa, she builds tools that let non-technical policy analysts run their own code-based analyses — on numbers they can trust and results they can reproduce. Her work sits at the seam between rigorous social research methods and modern computational tooling, exploring how expert judgment can be packaged into systems that analysts and AI agents can both use well.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Principles for Effective Interactive Visualizations
2026-09-16.description: Many interactive visualizations start from what libraries make easy like allowing hovering, brushing, and zooming rather than what analysis actually needs. The result is dashboards that look interactive but rarely change how people think about their data. This talk presents principles for designing meaningful interaction: how to identify which dimensions reward interactivity, how affordance design shapes user behavior, and how interactive composition can deepen exploration. We ground these ideas in live notebook examples and introduce vibewidget, an open-source Python library built on anywidget, that uses natural language to rapidly prototype interactive visualizations, making it practical to test and refine interaction ideas in real time.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Crying, Caching, and Compiling: The Five Stages of R Optimization
2026-09-16.description:
Is slow code giving you grief? Try working through the five stages:
1. Denial: My code WORKS. My tests are PASSING. Fine, I’ll try profiling.
2. Anger: dplyr::mutate() is that slow?!
3. Bargaining (aka caching): If I just store more in memory, then I don’t have to deal with compute time.
4. Depression: R is an interpreted language. Sometimes those are just slow. emo::ji(“sad”)
5. Acceptance: I’ll rewrite one critical function in Rust. Hope I don’t have to edit it later.
This presentation will guide non-programmers through speeding up their R code ranging from simple programming principles to incorporating Rust. Using examples from optimizing our tidywater package, you’ll learn to make code faster without sacrificing readability (too much).

2026-09-16.sessionName: Developing the developer
It Worked Great Until I Left
2026-09-16.description:
Recently I completed a project that I was really proud of. It worked great, and stakeholders were happy. Then I went on paternity leave, and the process I had built proved to be too complex to be handed off: everything broke. The underlying data wouldn't populate and the report wouldn't run. It took me returning to work to get everything back up and running.

This is a cautionary tale of how I let complexity creep in, how defaulting to familiar tools made my system harder to maintain, and how stepping back allowed me to identify the right tool for the job and simplify things. It is a reminder to build for the future maintainer and to always listen to the voice in your head that says "there has to be an easier way to do this."

speakers.title: Senior Power Analyst, Seattle City Light

2026-09-16.sessionName: Prepare locally, run remotely: Easily scale Tidymodels on Databricks with sparklyr
2026-09-16.description:
Historically, accelerating large grid searches meant moving to expensive grid computing or complex "do-it-yourself" Spark clusters. Even with the infrastructure, it usually required changing R code significantly to make it work. These barriers make it hard for a practitioner to justify the cost of money and effort in their daily work.

Today, Databricks has made high-performance Spark clusters easy to manage. In this session, we demonstrate how to off-load tuning jobs from a local R session to Databricks. Using the exact same Tidymodels objects, sparklyr automatically performs model evaluation in a parallel and distributed manner. Practitioners can now easily accelerate large grid searches at scale without refactoring.

2026-09-16.sessionName: AI in Data Science
How I Automated My Job, Cashed Out and Developed 6-Pack Abs Using AI!
2026-09-16.description: It's hard to balance the skepticism that comes from the assault of social media-based AI hype with the fear of missing out and becoming obsolete. Am I falling behind? Can AI do all my coding better than I can? Who is this Lang and why do I keep hearing about their chain? We've all been in meetings where management wants to see ROI from AI investments, and we've all had to navigate vendors promising the world and coming up short. In this talk, I will give some actionable insights for navigating the fast-paced space, some pitfalls that I've experienced and how to extract true value from the perspective of an average data scientist at a pharmaceutical company just trying to level up his kid's college fund.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Roll for Wisdom: What AI Gets Wrong About Data Analysis
2026-09-16.description:
AI tools have been excellent for writing software. We can turn an agent loose and feel relatively confident that we can achieve a good result since we can verify changes via unit tests. 

However, it often falls flat for some types of data analysis. I think the reason is a lack of understanding of what a bad idea is and other aspects of common sense. The situation is similar to D&D's conceptions of intelligence versus wisdom: raw facts versus reason. 

I'll give some examples of: poor data analysis choices, information leakage, and overfitting to its training set.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Fake it Til' You Make It: Mocking Reality So Your Tests Can Run
2026-09-16.description:
As data scientists mature in their work, many move from analysis scripts to larger codebases and packages, bringing unit testing into the workflow. For some, a handful of basic tests is enough. For others, as code grows more complex, familiar testing patterns may start to break.

We’ll explore testing in isolation as a practical way to handle more challenging programming scenarios. We’ll cover the core ideas behind mocking and controlling your code’s environment while focusing on when, where, how, and why these techniques help in real projects. The talk is intended for anyone already comfortable with unit testing who wants to explore strategies for isolating behavior, reducing test fragility, and expanding test coverage for complex systems.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Keynote Session: Navigating the Agentic Future
2026-09-16.description: Agents are taking over a growing share of day to day coding work. As models and harnesses continue to improve, where are we still needed? What skills must we develop to be effective and successful in this agent-powered future? In this talk I'll share my perspective after more than a year of using agents to create many large new codebases for software engineering and data work. I'll make the case that the things that have always mattered—human agency, good taste, and architectural thinking—are still what will determine whether we succeed or fail.

speakers.title: Principal Architect, Posit
speakers.description: Wes is an entrepreneur and software developer focusing on analytical computing. He is currently a Principal Architect at Posit. He previously created or co-created the Python pandas, Ibis, and Apache Arrow open source projects. More recently, Wes has delved into agentic software engineering with the roborev and msgvault projects, supporting continuous code review and secure, private email storage and search for AI agents. He is a frequent speaker at conferences and is a co-host of The Test Set, a data science podcast from Posit.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Three Agents, Two Mistakes, or Designing for LLM-Assisted Data Analysis
2026-09-16.description:
We've built three data science agents at Posit over the last eighteen months, each one a correction of the last. Positron Assistant was focused just on writing code itself, and so was too rigid to keep up with the iterative work of data science. Databot lacked the depth needed for start-to-finish workflows because it was an expert in one thing, exploratory data analysis. Posit Assistant is what we built once we understood what we needed both: a fast, flexible coding agent that is also an expert in data science.

This talk is about the design decisions in between each iteration, and why the harness around a model matters more than the model inside it. Each mistake taught us part of why: every data science feature we added to a generic coding agent made that agent harder to change, and an agent's autonomy is only as good as what it has access to.

The demos are in Positron; the principles aren't.

speakers.title: Software Engineer, Posit, PBC
speakers.description:
Sam builds user-first features for the Positron IDE. He may be writing in TypeScript and Rust now, but deep down, he has a Python soul. 

At Posit, he spent several months helping lay the groundwork for AI integration within Positron before transitioning to more database-focused workflows and integrations. Before that, he built control interfaces and data analysis tools for the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider at Brookhaven National Laboratory. 

When he isn't reflecting on the evolution of AI tools for data science, he’s usually cooking, snapping landscapes on his Sony a6400 (rollerblades optional, but encouraged), or spending time with his cats, Missy and Mabel.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Between Code and Conclusions: An Evaluation Layer for LLM-Generated Analysis
2026-09-16.description: LLMs quickly analyze data, but they routinely violate statistical assumptions, ignore missing data patterns, and misinterpret what variables actually measure. In this talk, I'll show how Circuit, an evaluation layer for LLM-generated data analysis, catches these mistakes before they reach users. We built an API and semantic layer that sits between code execution and output, using R as a first-class language to detect both statistical errors (assumption violations, selection bias, ignored uncertainty) and ontological errors (misunderstanding what data means). You'll see real examples of failures Circuit prevents, learn how the architecture works, and leave with patterns for building guardrails into your own AI-assisted workflows.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Staying Organized Across Machines: Practical Workflows for Data Scientists with Busy Brains
2026-09-16.description: Data science work can be chaotic even on a good day — and when you’re juggling multiple clients, multiple machines, and an ADHD brain, organization becomes mission‑critical. In this talk, I’ll share a cognitive‑friendly workflow built around Obsidian, Git, and reproducible R and Python projects that helps me stay focused and consistent across contexts. I’ll walk through how I manage cross‑machine notes, secure client information, integrate Obsidian tasks with Outlook calendars, and use Templater and backlinks to keep fast, messy notes connected to long‑term structure.Attendees will leave with lightweight, copy‑ready templates and habits they can use to stay organized — even when balancing complex projects, clients, and busy brains.

speakers.title: Sr. Strategic Services Analyst, DeepSeas
speakers.description:
I'm a strategic data scientist who helps teams make sense of messy, complex data. My current role focuses on defining metrics, building reporting pipelines, and identifying the right measures to track organizational goals and highlight team impact, turning ambiguity into clear, actionable insight leadership can act on.

I enjoy partnering across organizations, delivering training, and developing fun (to me anyway!) visualizations and tools. Outside of work, I'm passionate about organizational systems, reading science fiction, and running outdoors.

If you're working on something interesting or just want to connect, feel free to reach out!

2026-09-16.sessionName: Building Confidence, Not Bugs: Internal Packages for Empowered Data Teams
2026-09-16.description:
This talk details how I moved the team's core business logic from scattered scripts into a robust, version-controlled internal package to prevent recurrence. I will cover the transition from copy-paste to package maintenance and testing, and the importance of demystifying tool-building for non-engineers.
I will cover:
- Identifying when code needs a function, and when a function needs a package.
- Strategies for consistently hard-coding domain knowledge (e.g., categorizations, identifiers, offsets).
- Reduced onboarding time and increased confidence for junior team members—a major cultural win.
You will receive a roadmap for building their first internal package and the confidence to treat analysis code as the software product it is.

2026-09-16.sessionName: When English Is Second, R Comes First
2026-09-16.description: English is my second language, and for years that meant hesitation in professional settings. I often had strong ideas but not always the words. In R, I found fluency. Through tools like ggplot2, Shiny, and Quarto, I discovered a language of precision where data visualization and interactive workflows communicate ideas clearly. This talk explores how the R ecosystem becomes more than a toolkit — it becomes a platform for confidence, community, and expression, showing how code can serve as a powerful medium for communication, not just computation.

speakers.title: Data Scientist at FNBO (First National Bank of Omaha)

2026-09-16.sessionName: Creating Ergonomic Informatics Solutions to Enhance Patient Care in the Digital Health Era
2026-09-16.description: In the current digital health era, the need for rapid insights is nearing the expectation of real-time delivery. We present our experience developing on-demand data science pipelines atop the electronic medical record. Specifically, the topics of our use case examples focus on: 1) the utilization of continuous health monitoring data extracted from wearable devices in the inpatient setting, as well as, 2) the analytical environments leveraged to process high-volume signal measurements (e.g., sleep-wake patterns, actigraphy, sensory exposures). In alignment with learning health systems (LHS) models, our work demonstrates how informatics-driven insights can be harnessed to implement patient-centered workflow changes directly at the bedside.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Keynote Session: Context is the Control Plane
2026-09-16.description: Context has always been critical to applied data work – long before artificial intelligence made it a buzzword. But why aren’t we nearly as intentional when curating context for ourselves as for agents? This talk will explore the many types of context data scientists require to do meaningful work – from the unarticulated questions motivating our work, the mechanics of the source systems responsible for delivering our data, the assumptions baked into every one of our tools, the tacit knowledge hidden from view in parallel disciplines, and the way we share our findings. Along the way, we will discuss practical tips for building and curating the context needed for data work and how this process is part of what keeps our field fundamentally creative and human.

speakers.title: Senior Manager of Data Science, Capital One
speakers.description:
Emily Riederer is a data scientist at Capital One where she leads the development of specialty underwriting models and serves as a Model Risk Officer for fraud models. 

Over the past decade, Emily has worn all the hats in the data space with work spanning analysis (inference and measurement), engineering (analyst tools, data pipelines, data products), and science (core machine learning). She is passionate about bridging the gaps between these disciplines. While navigating large enterprise settings, Emily has also served as a “data team of one” for many pro-bono projects and data-driven voter turnout initiatives. 

Outside of work, Emily enjoys supporting open source software and the free flow of information. She promotes open science by serving on the editorial board of rOpenSci, on the technical advisory board of Bluebonnet Data, and as a volunteer statistical textbook reviewer for Routledge / CRC Press. Her own writing and past talks center on developing reproducible workflows and exposing the tacit knowledge of data work and can be found on her website https://www.emilyriederer.com/.

2026-09-16.sessionName: Lunch & Birds of a Feather Meetups
Lunch & Learn with AWS: Using Positron & Amazon Sagemaker for Regulated Industries
2026-09-16.description:
Traditional analysis work is spread across tools that aren’t always compatible. The data sits in a warehouse you reach through an extract. The model runs on another platform. The results end up as a screenshot in someone else's deck.

Join us for a live walkthrough of how Positron, running natively on Amazon SageMaker, can act as a central hub for end-to-end analysis.

Positron is a capable IDE for working through data science and analysis tasks. Posit Assistant, in this case backed by Amazon Bedrock, helps us get our bearings in a synthetic loan dataset, writing queries against Athena as we go. Since everything from the data to the foundational AI models are AWS native, nothing leaves the boundary your organization already trusts.

Once we have our bearings on the data, we’ll focus on a single question. We’ll explore the data, train a model, keep a record of everything we tried, deploy the best model somewhere it can be called, and publish a report to Posit Connect that fetches the current numbers on a schedule. All from the comfort of Positron on SageMaker.
